Dedication

This book is dedicated to my teachers — in school, at university, at work and in life — and to my mother, Veena, and my father, Nand Kumar, for teaching me the most consequential lessons in life.

Epigraph

"Every company is going to be an AI company."

— Jensen Huang, co-founder and CEO, NVIDIA

Preface

I have built data and machine-learning systems for technology companies. I have watched AI move from making narrow predictions to helping people write software, investigate problems and carry out sequences of work. That change fascinates me. It also makes me careful about what a model appears to understand. How does a system trained to predict language become useful at reasoning through a problem? What has it learned, and when might a convincing answer mislead us?

The question that brings me back is larger than any particular model capability: what happens to a world when problem solving becomes abundant?

An answer can be plentiful while the means to act on it remain scarce. But if examining a problem, or trying to develop a useful tool, becomes affordable to many more people, we should expect more than a faster version of familiar work. We should look again at the work we have not yet attempted, the people we have not served and the institutions we have not yet built.

Training teaches these systems patterns that can be useful far beyond the examples they encountered. Some of their answers suggest that they have learned relationships about how parts of the world work, rather than merely familiar phrases. How reliable that understanding is remains an open question. I do not need to settle it to feel the force of what is happening. A system that helps someone examine a difficult problem, write a useful program or coordinate a sequence of actions changes the work available to them. When many people and institutions gain that capacity, the consequences reach into the physical world.

I think of this as a Great Force of our time. Something so consequential that it changes what deserves our attention. The possibilities extend toward discoveries that relieve suffering, and the dangers include damage we cannot readily reverse. Neither destination is guaranteed. The people building and using these systems make these choices, but no individual stands at a complete set of controls. Ownership, competition, public institutions, habits and accidents also shape what follows. Part of leadership is discovering where one's authority ends, then helping build the arrangements that are missing.

I am writing for the finite person who must decide in the presence of this force. Flesh and bone, prone to fatigue and bias, sometimes confident and at other times anxious. I am one of those people. Across the screen, an AI system can seem to offer inexhaustible answers, each convincingly argued. We still have one working day, obligations to particular people and decisions that will not wait for certainty. More answers do not settle which ones deserve our commitment.

I want this book to be a field guide for leading yourself, other people and an organisation as AI becomes part of ordinary life. It should help you understand what is changing and practise the judgment needed to act under pressure. More capable tools will still leave you with choices to make and results to answer for. The work includes recognising when a polished answer is unreliable, giving people a clear direction and correcting mistakes.

I began writing this book to understand this change while it was still forming. That remains the purpose of the book. It offers principles I would want to remain useful even if progress accelerates, slows down, becomes expensive, or takes a direction we failed to anticipate. It does not claim to have found the permanent border between human and machine capability. Such a border would be a poor foundation for building your business and for life.

The revolution arrives in an organisation on an ordinary working day. One person sees a chance to automate a frustrating task. Another is told to produce the same results with a smaller team. A third is judged by a score they cannot explain. People can live under decisions shaped by AI without ever using the tool themselves. A leader must understand those experiences as well as the possibilities that first made the technology exciting.

All this does not require us to become timid. The possibilities should energise us: building services that were previously unaffordable, finding answers that were previously out of reach, and creating organisations in which more people can contribute. It also includes choosing which promises deserve the money, attention and power needed to make them real. Concern for people becomes serious when it changes those choices.

The book begins with foundations: value, human motives and mastery. It then turns inward, to what a leader wants, doubts and needs to let go of. From there we move to the work, the people doing it, their relationships, new opportunities and the institutions that will outlast a particular leader. The nine sections belong together. Skill without a worthwhile purpose can make damage more efficient. Purpose without competence can make promises other people must repair. Competence and purpose without limits can become a private rule over lives the leader does not own.

I have tried to make the principles answerable to situations rather than decorate situations with principles. There are decisions here without a clean winner. There are workers who disagree for good reasons, and workers whose predictions prove mistaken without making their interests illegitimate. There are projects worth attempting that fail their first test. A person can do something valuable without securing a grateful ending.

My own starting point is that leadership stems from knowing the truth without performative decoration or unnecessary sophistication, and from delivering it simply. That asks something of the leader before it asks anything of the listener. We have to find out what is happening. We have to distinguish what we know from what we want to be true. And when the facts change, we have to correct the account we have given other people.

Here is one expectation I will test in this book: many people may gain useful AI assistance without keeping much of the income it helps create. That is especially likely where a few firms control something else they need, such as access to customers, essential infrastructure or capital, and changing providers is difficult. I will also examine the contrary case: when competition gives customers better terms and helps workers or smaller firms retain more of the gain. If workers and smaller firms consistently retained a growing share of the financial gains despite those barriers, I would need to reconsider the explanation.

Who keeps the gain affects the choices available to everyone else: whether shorter hours are affordable, who can negotiate a changed job, and whether people can challenge decisions made about them. These are consequences a leader needs to examine, not leave hidden inside a claim that the business has become more productive.

Among the lives this change will affect, I think most about people expected to follow decisions they had little part in making. Many may never read this book. Whether it was worth writing will show up in what happens to them.

Rahul Kapil

Before You Begin

Throughout this book, we will return to Northline, a fictional regional logistics firm. Northline is a literary device: a continuing business story through which we can examine what a leadership principle asks of people in practice. Instead of starting with a new company whenever the subject changes, we will stay with an organisation long enough to see the consequences of its decisions.

That continuity matters. A faster booking process can change the work of a customer-service team. A new service can create an opportunity for a customer and a difficult afternoon for dispatch. A promise made by the person running the business can become an obligation somebody else has to fulfil. Following the same people lets us see these connections, including the consequences that remain after a chapter's immediate question has been answered.

Northline, its people, its customers and their conversations are invented for this purpose. They are not reported interviews, disguised research or episodes from my career. The story makes decisions concrete; it does not establish how frequently they occur in the world. Research and historical examples are identified in the notes. Monetary examples are expressed in dollars ($) and use stated simplifying assumptions, not market prices or forecasts.

The business we will follow

Northline collects and delivers goods across a region. Some customers send regular consignments; others call when a part has stopped a job, a workshop has something ready to ship or an earlier arrangement has fallen through. Customers want their goods moved at a time they can rely on. Northline has to make that promise fit its vehicles, drivers, loading space, money and existing commitments.

It is an ordinary operating business with an interesting possibility in front of it. Small workshops need dependable collections, but the calls, planning and exceptions attached to each account have made them expensive to serve. If AI reduces part of that work, a service Northline previously rejected may become worth attempting. The cost of preparing an answer can change before the cost of keeping the promise does.

Northline's first workshop trial fails. The consequences continue through later decisions about services and relationships, while separate improvements to ordinary work change jobs and coverage. A later attempt succeeds within limits. We will follow what the company learns, what it gets wrong and what its people are asked to carry along the way.

Meet the people

Peter runs Northline. He is responsible for its direction and for the commitments the business takes on. He knows customers by name, enjoys finding a way to solve their problems and sees possibilities quickly. He wants Northline to grow into a more useful business; sometimes his confidence gets ahead of the operation's ability to deliver.

Ava guards the money and budget. She examines what an experiment will cost and what the company can afford to promise. She is precise, sceptical of attractive forecasts and willing to fund uncertainty when its terms are visible. She wants the business to remain able to honour its obligations, though her preference for another check can impose costs she has not counted.

Thomas builds and connects the systems. He makes software work with the information and exceptions Northline actually encounters. He is curious, practical and excited by what AI lets him attempt. He wants to build useful things and make the operation work better; his pride in what he has built can make buying somebody else's solution harder to consider fairly.

Shaun champions the customer. He handles requests, difficult conversations and the difference between what a message says and what its recipient thinks it promises. He likes finding a way to say yes and dislikes asking a customer to repair Northline's confusion. He wants dependable service and work he can take pride in, on terms he can sustain in his own life.

Sunder keeps dispatch moving. He fits collections and deliveries around available capacity and commitments already made. He notices the small change that can rearrange an afternoon. He wants promises that the operation can keep, and enough authority to settle a conflict before somebody has made it more expensive.

Dennis works the depot floor. He handles the physical work behind the plan and notices when a neat instruction ignores weight, space or the conditions of a shift. He is direct, observant and sometimes attached to a familiar method after its original reason has gone. He wants the work done properly and the people doing it judged fairly.

Maya joins the service team as a trainee. She learns to interpret requests and recognise when an ordinary-looking case needs a different decision. She is comfortable trying new tools, but speed can make her work appear more settled than her understanding. She wants to become capable of handling real responsibility, not merely producing convincing replies.

Nadia is an experienced service colleague. She takes on paid later coverage and becomes an alternate supervisor for Maya. She is attentive to what a customer needs next and willing to leave an uncertainty plainly stated. She wants to resolve the case she is holding, with clear authority and working hours that the organisation respects.

Miriam is a board director. She helps organise the scrutiny of consequential commitments and the board's response when an approved plan fails. She asks what an assurance is based on and what the decision actually permits. She wants ambition supported by evidence and accountability, including accountability for the board's own choices.

Elise runs a carrier in an adjoining area. She brings an independent business into cooperation with Northline. She is commercially practical and clear about what she has agreed to do. She wants worthwhile work on terms that preserve her company's independence; Peter's enthusiasm does not give him authority over her people or capacity.

These people want a business that works. That agreement leaves plenty to disagree about. Their responsibilities, interests and knowledge give them different views of the same event. None is here to be right every time, and understanding another person's reasons need not make the disagreement disappear.

What Northline has

Northline adds AI to particular parts of its work over time. Thomas builds some applications and the company buys others. You do not need to memorise these tools. This table is a reference for when one reappears later in the story. It distinguishes AI applications from the ordinary records and software they use.

What it is What it does Where it comes from First appears
The AI quotation assistant drafts replies to enquiries built in-house Ch. 1
The fleet record ordinary records used to check vehicle availability before confirming a collection existing system, opened up to more people Ch. 1
The AI loading-plan assistant proposes how to load a vehicle built in-house Ch. 3
The shared booking view one record of agreed booking details, visible to service and dispatch; the shared record is ordinary software within the wider AI-assisted booking process built in-house Ch. 7
The context notes stored operational notes used by the AI when it proposes a booking decision built in-house Ch. 8
The AI booking-change flow makes ordinary amendments within limits and stops outside them built in-house Ch. 9
The operating summary the depot's weekly measures, including the handling target, prepared with AI assistance built in-house Ch. 11
The supplier's AI booking assistant interprets booking requests in a customer’s own words; the surrounding software checks whether a booking may be confirmed bought from a supplier Ch. 16
The AI route generator produces and compares candidate routes cheaply built in-house Ch. 19
The handover view the record shared with Elise's carrier, prepared with AI assistance on both sides built with a partner Ch. 20
The acceptance check ordinary software that checks the booking record for the receiving supplier’s current acceptance of a return built in-house Ch. 19

Alongside these applications, people at Northline use a general-purpose AI assistant: a chatbot in which they type questions, compare ideas and ask for drafts or explanations. A personal conversation with that assistant does not change a customer’s booking. An application connected to Northline’s records may be allowed to act, but only within the permissions the company gives it. Each scene identifies which kind of use is involved.

The workshop collection service is something Northline sells, not a piece of software. Its first trial, serving scattered workshops, ends in Chapter 10 because the proposed price does not cover the cost. A more compact service, with customers close together, is tested in Chapter 18. The translation pilot in Chapter 10 is a separate, hypothetical business example.

AI can interpret a customer’s message, draft a reply or suggest a plan. Ordinary software can look up a record, enforce a permission or save an accepted change. People decide what the business may promise. These activities often sit inside the same application, but the story distinguishes them because a failure in one calls for a different remedy from a failure in another.

The chapters also address you directly and draw on other workplaces, hypothetical examples and identified research. Those passages extend the lesson beyond one fictional company. When the narrative returns to Northline, it names the people and decision we are returning to.

How to use the book

Read the Northline scenes for the choices people make and the consequences they face. Use the wider examples and questions to examine a decision in your own setting.

The book is addressed first to leaders of operating businesses and teams, including technology organisations. “AI native” describes familiarity with a set of capabilities. It confers no rank in human worth and no automatic qualification to govern.

You do not need a software background. The chapters distinguish what a model contributes from the information, ordinary software and authority needed to put its output to work. Optional technical background appears at the end.

Read the first time for the sequence. Return later to a decision you actually face. The question is not whether a sentence sounds right when underlined. It is whether you can state what it requires, who bears its cost, what evidence would alter it and who may challenge your application of it.

The situation index points from a predicament to a chapter and aid. Working pages are optional; use them within your authority. A principle should improve your sight, never become an excuse to stop looking.

Section I · What Does Not Change

Value, motives, and competence

1. Scarcity Moves, and Value Follows It

Northline is a regional logistics firm with vans, drivers, a depot and a service desk that arranges collections for local businesses. Peter runs the company; Thomas builds and maintains its software. Thomas has connected an AI quotation assistant to incoming customer enquiries. It reads a request and drafts a priced reply for the service team to check. This morning, Peter is looking at the time it saves and what happens when replies become ready faster than dispatch can confirm the work.

By ten that morning, the AI assistant had prepared replies for a quotation queue that usually kept the service team busy until lunch. Staff still had to check each reply before sending it.

Thomas turned his screen towards Peter. The quotation assistant could read a customer's request, extract the collection details, consult the rate table and prepare a reply. A member of the service team checked it before sending. The awkward requests still needed attention. The ordinary ones moved quickly.

Peter picked an example. Two cartons, a familiar address, collection that afternoon. The price was right. The message was clear. He could see several uses for the hours they were going to recover.

In the old process, the employee preparing a quote usually called dispatch before offering a collection window. Drafting took long enough that those calls reached Sunder, who ran dispatch, gradually. Now requests were reaching dispatch faster than he could clear them. The new workflow therefore allowed the service team to confirm straightforward jobs from the fleet record, which showed which vehicles were free, sending only exceptions to him.

Then Sunder came in from dispatch.

“Which vehicle have we promised for the repair shop?”

Thomas opened the booking. “The smaller van is available.”

“The van is here. Its driver isn't.”

The fleet record was accurate about the vehicle. It said nothing about the driver covering another route. The person checking the quote had checked the information on the screen. The customer had received a collection window and arranged the afternoon around it.

Shaun, who looked after customers, made the next call. He could offer a later collection. The customer could not be there later. Sunder began looking for another way to fit the job into the day.

Ordinary requests no longer waited for a reply to be drafted. They waited for someone to confirm that Northline could do the job. The fleet shortcut hid part of this problem: some bookings bypassed the capacity check, while others queued for dispatch.

Find the constraint that moved

When a difficult activity becomes cheap, our first impulse is to do more of it. More proposals, more analysis, more designs, more conversations with prospective customers. The resulting work can be useful and still arrive faster than colleagues can examine it, customers can act on it or the operation can fulfil the promises it invites people to make. The constraint has moved.

At Northline, the quotation process had contained several kinds of work. Someone interpreted a request, checked a price, established whether the collection was feasible and communicated the offer. Those activities looked like one task because one person often did them together. The AI drafted replies faster, but it lacked some of the information needed to decide whether Northline could keep the promise.

It would have been easy to respond by returning every quote to Sunder. Sunder could check capacity before each offer went out, but the new queue would form at his desk. Northline would then call him a bottleneck, although it had designed the work to require his attention.

Instead, Thomas and Sunder examined what needed checking. An ordinary collection with confirmed capacity could proceed through a simpler path. A request involving uncertain availability needed an operational decision before it became a promise. They also needed one place where a capacity reservation became visible to the next person making an offer. Two individually sensible quotes could otherwise promise the same remaining space.

By the end of the following week, requests whose capacity had already been confirmed were moving through cleanly. Unusual collection windows still waited for Sunder. Peter postponed the upgrade that would generate more elaborate quotes. Thomas’s next task was to give the service team the information and rules to confirm routine capacity without calling dispatch. Sunder would handle cases those rules did not cover. The remaining work had changed what deserved the next week of development.

The constraint might be distribution, a machine, a customer's willingness to change a habit, or demand itself. Suppose Northline had spare vehicles and promptly answered every enquiry, but few customers wanted another collection. Hiring another dispatcher would not fix that problem. It would add cost to capacity the company could not sell. If useful orders were instead waiting for someone to reconcile available routes, that same hire might be worthwhile. The right investment depends on which fact limits delivery.

Do not assume that “human judgment” must be the next scarce resource; AI can assist judgment too. Nor is every shortage worth solving. For Northline, relieving a constraint must improve a service customers will pay enough to sustain. In other settings, the worthwhile outcome may be different. A shortage of attention to an unwanted proposal is not automatically a reason to fund it.

What the saved time is worth

Back at Northline, Ava, who managed the budget, asked what they intended to do with the time recovered from ordinary quotes.

Peter suggested counting it as a saving.

“Whose cost has changed?” she asked.

Staff were still employed for the same hours. The firm had bought software and spent Thomas's time on the integration. There could be a return, but it had not yet arrived as lower payroll.

Freed time can be valuable without becoming cash. Clearing a backlog, resolving a customer's dispute and leaving work at the hour you were meant to leave are benefits someone can recognise. These benefits should be recorded separately. Time spent clearing a backlog cannot also be counted as time spent serving new customers. Additional revenue requires demand for that service; lower payroll requires an actual reduction in paid work, with consequences for the people affected. Relief of a constraint makes a choice possible. It does not supply the next source of demand.

Shaun wanted time to follow up unresolved customer problems. Peter wanted to respond to more enquiries. Ava asked them to look at the open cases before dividing the supposed gain.

Several customers had called twice about the same matter. Answering each call counted as completed work; leaving the matter unresolved generated the next call. Shaun could point to a customer who was withholding another booking until an earlier collection dispute was settled.

Peter agreed to give the recovered time to clearing those cases for a fortnight. They would check repeat calls and completed resolutions, not merely how quickly the phone was answered. More sales enquiries would wait.

In his update to the team, he changed the claim. “We've made ordinary quotes faster. We haven't reduced our costs yet. We're using the time to finish customer problems we've been leaving open.”

Research on general-purpose technologies offers a useful warning here. Brynjolfsson, Rock and Syverson describe how investments in processes, business arrangements and skills can accompany the adoption of a new technology, with effects that are poorly captured by immediate productivity measures.[1] This gives a leader a reason to examine the complementary work a new tool requires. It gives no firm an exemption from showing that its own investment is useful.

Who receives the gain?

Suppose the revised system works and Northline can handle ordinary requests with less effort. At first, a prompt, dependable offer may win business from slower competitors. If those competitors acquire the same capability, customers may come to expect the quicker service. Where customers can compare and switch readily, carriers may have to pass some of the saving on through prices or better terms. The improvement can remain valuable to customers while ceasing to earn Northline an extra margin.

In that case, Peter's reason to invest changes. Faster quotation becomes part of remaining competitive. Earning more requires another useful difference, perhaps a service the old administrative cost made uneconomic. A supplier's increased charge or employees' negotiated share could change the distribution again. There is no universal percentage that belongs to the person who first improved the task.

Creating value means producing a benefit: the workshop owner spends less time arranging transport, an employee finishes an unresolved case, the carrier carries a load at lower cost. Capturing value means retaining a share through income, margin or favourable terms. Someone may benefit without Northline earning more; Northline may earn more without increasing the pay of the people who made it possible.

During that first fortnight, fewer repeat calls and more resolved cases would show whether the saved time helped customers. They would not establish a payroll saving or a lasting increase in profit.

Later, Northline’s returns would also depend on its customers, suppliers and competitors. Peter could not control their decisions. He could examine those dependencies before treating a temporary advantage as permanent.

Look at what was previously too expensive

Most discussions of efficiency begin with work the organisation already performs. The larger opportunity may be waiting among the requests it declines.

Northline heard regularly from small workshops that needed dependable collections but sent too little freight to justify much administration. A single modest booking could generate several calls about timing, access and price. The goods might be easy to carry, yet arranging the collection could make the booking unprofitable before a vehicle even set out.

Cheaper coordination gave Peter a reason to reopen that question. It did not give him a viable service. The workshops might be too far apart. They might need incompatible collection times. What they were willing to pay might still fall below what Northline needed to charge.

Yet there was now something worth finding out. Could workshops in one area accept a fixed collection day? Would a simpler recurring arrangement remove enough effort for both sides? Could a workshop owner keep a working morning that was otherwise lost to arranging transport?

Even before changing the cost of delivery, the technology could change the cost of finding out. The team could organise requests, compare a few service designs and investigate whether a compact cluster existed without committing to a full launch. A cheaper inquiry was worth undertaking even if its answer turned out to be no. Finding a viable offer would still require attention to people whose needs were absent from the current revenue report.

Return to the repair-shop booking that began the chapter. Shaun found a time the customer could accept the following morning, and Sunder fitted it into a route with confirmed capacity. The owner still had to rearrange a job.

“Then why did you confirm today?” the owner asked.

Shaun explained the missed availability check and what they were changing. The customer listened, then asked him to send the new collection time in writing.

On Thomas’s screen, preparing the next quotation took seconds. That saving did not give the repair-shop owner back the afternoon Northline’s promise had cost him.

Notes

1. Erik Brynjolfsson, Daniel Rock and Chad Syverson, The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies, NBER Working Paper 25148, issued 2018 and revised 2020. The argument here uses the abstract's account of complementary intangible investment. No fixed adoption timetable or guaranteed payoff is inferred. Northline, its dialogue and its operational events are illustrative fiction.

2. The Animal at the Controls

Peter was considering a new collection service for small workshops. A competitor had begun advertising a similar offer. Before he had checked how it worked, Peter turned to a general-purpose AI chatbot for help planning Northline’s response. The question was whether he was investigating an opportunity or asking the chatbot to justify a decision he had already made.

Before breakfast, he typed his question into the AI assistant: how should Northline respond to the competitor? He did not ask whether it should respond at all.

A competing carrier was offering small businesses a simpler way to arrange collections. The page was polished, the explanation short. It suggested that a customer could obtain the sort of dependable service Northline had spent years treating as difficult to provide economically.

Peter ran Northline. He knew the difficulty was real. He also knew that difficulties could become comfortable explanations for leaving a market alone.

In his prompt, Peter described Northline’s strengths, the opportunity and the danger of moving too slowly. The AI assistant turned that urgency into a convincing plan, with stages, responsibilities and a commercial argument. By the time he reached the depot, his impulse looked like a considered proposal.

Ava, who managed the money, read it.

“What have the workshops asked for?”

“Reliable collections. Less administration. We've discussed this.”

“And what changed this morning?”

Peter showed her the announcement.

The competitor might have found a better way to operate. It might have written a better description of an ordinary service. Peter did not yet know. He had nevertheless asked the AI assistant to explain why Northline needed to accelerate, and it had done what he asked.

Plain language alone does not make a leader truthful. I can explain a decision clearly and still leave out the facts that would challenge it. Before asking an AI assistant to develop my argument, I need to admit which outcome I already want. Then I need evidence that could make me choose differently.

Relief can feel like a reason

Urgency is not the only feeling an AI assistant can turn into a convincing argument. After a day spent dealing with other people’s difficulties, you may simply want one decision to stop being difficult.

Imagine the proposal arriving while you are trying to finish work. The AI assistant has answered your objections, supplied a plausible comparison and written the message announcing the choice; a colleague is waiting, somebody at home is waiting, and approving the recommendation would release you from both the task and the discomfort of remaining undecided. Relief has become part of the offer.

There is no fixed hour after which your judgment becomes unreliable, and important decisions will not always wait until you are rested. Your organisation needs a way to share or defer decisions when someone is exhausted, before a mistake exposes the problem.

If a consequential choice can wait, give yourself time to examine the evidence again before committing. If it cannot, decide what must be settled now and ask a colleague to check the uncertainty with the largest consequences. Be clear about who can make the final decision. Show that colleague what is still unknown, rather than a polished case for agreeing with you.

Sometimes the honest sentence is: I can deal with the immediate problem, but I cannot responsibly settle the larger one tonight. You need an organisation in which somebody can say that to you as well.

A good argument for the wrong question

A useful reasoning tool can improve a decision. It can also supply convincing reasons for a decision we have already made on impulse.

Back at Northline, Peter’s morning plan did not require any manipulation by the chatbot. He supplied the direction. The AI assistant supplied a structure in which that direction made sense. If he had asked why Northline should protect its existing customers before expanding, he might have received an equally coherent argument for restraint.

Neither answer would settle the business question. Each would demonstrate what could be said from a particular starting point.

Peter wanted to serve customers and grow Northline, but he also wanted to avoid discovering that another carrier had solved a problem he had declared uneconomic, and beneath that embarrassment lay the pleasure he took in being first. All of these could inhabit the same sentence about strategic urgency. Mixed motives did not disqualify him from deciding. They made it necessary to let a fact arrive that his preferred account had left out.

Consider the difference between two questions. “How do we capture this opportunity before competitors?” assumes an opportunity worth capturing and makes speed the organising concern. “What would have to be true for this service to deserve our next investment?” leaves room for a different conclusion. Both can be useful. They do different work.

Let the inconvenient fact arrive

Ava did not ask Peter to stop being competitive. Northline needed someone who cared whether another carrier had become more useful. She asked him to separate two things: what the announcement established, and what it made him feel. His urgency was real. It was not yet evidence that Northline should accelerate.

They put four short statements above the plan.

Northline had recurring enquiries from small workshops. Its present way of serving them consumed too much individual attention. A rival was advertising an offer they had not investigated. Peter wanted to move sooner than he had wanted to move yesterday.

Shaun learned of a real deadline when he spoke to a workshop association. It was comparing collection arrangements for its next planning period, including the rival’s fixed-day offer, and wanted Northline’s answer within six weeks. Its members would not wait indefinitely.

Peter had been right that delay could cost something. He had not been entitled to infer the size or nature of that cost from the announcement alone.

The distinction changed the action. Northline needed a credible answer within six weeks. It did not need to promise an unrestricted launch immediately. The deadline justified focused investigation and a bounded proposal. It did not justify pretending that capacity and economics had already been resolved.

The leader's private incentives become other people's working conditions

A person using an AI assistant to organise a holiday can waste a day defending an unsuitable itinerary. A leader can turn an equivalent mistake into a quarter of other people's work.

Peter’s excitement could set Thomas’s development priorities, shape Shaun’s customer promises and create a new problem for Sunder in dispatch. Once their work began, changing direction would become more expensive. Peter would have to cancel work, explain the change to customers and account for money already spent. His preference at breakfast could become a commitment other people had to fulfil.

It is also why asking for objections is insufficient. Someone may know the relevant fact and still conclude that stating it is expensive. If a leader celebrates speed and calls every constraint a failure of imagination, people can learn to keep constraints out of the room. An AI assistant does not need to create that condition. It can simply make the leader's account more difficult to interrupt.

The temptation to outsource your opposition

You can ask an AI system to argue against your plan. Often you should. It can surface alternatives you have overlooked and help you understand why a reasonable person might disagree.

But you still choose the information it sees. If you reject the inconvenient objection as irrelevant, change the prompt until the response becomes agreeable and accept a weak counterargument because it is easy to defeat, you can finish the exercise feeling challenged while retaining control of everything that challenged you. It becomes a private debate in which you appoint both sides and the judge.

Bring at least one important claim into contact with something that does not depend on your framing. A customer's actual choice, a capacity record, an unpaid invoice or a colleague with authority to refuse can provide that contact. Their evidence may itself need interpretation. It nevertheless has a source beyond the coherence of your conversation with the tool.

A record you can return to

Before asking a tool to justify a consequential move, write what you presently think the decision is. State what is known, what you want, what you fear and what observation could change the choice. Keep it short enough that you cannot hide the important part in the surrounding prose.

Then use the tool to explore options, identify costs and develop alternatives. Return to the record you wrote beforehand. It will help you see whether the conversation changed your view or merely supplied better arguments for it. Has the evidence changed the decision, or has the language merely made the initial preference more impressive?

After the team had examined the plan, Peter replaced the launch date at the top of his plan with the association's decision deadline. He asked Shaun to establish the service its members would actually use, and Thomas to identify what could be tested within that period. The plan became less triumphant and more useful.

He kept the competitor's announcement. Later, opening it to check a detail, he caught himself admiring the page again. The plan had changed more quickly than the feeling.

3. What a Master Has Always Been

Thomas has begun using an AI loading-plan assistant to suggest the order in which goods should go into a vehicle. He brings a proposal to Dennis, who works on Northline’s depot floor and knows the route. They need to check whether the plan fits the actual load. Later, Thomas will face a similar question about his own work: which parts of the software he built are still worth keeping?

Thomas found it easier to question Dennis’s old methods than his own.

The proposed loading plan looked reasonable until Dennis examined the goods intended for the final stop.

Thomas had asked the AI loading-plan assistant to suggest a sequence for a mixed load. It listed the consignments neatly, put the first delivery within reach and appeared to respect the available space.

Dennis pointed to a heavy item placed above a carton that could not support it.

“That can't go there.”

Thomas corrected the instruction. The next plan avoided the problem. Dennis examined it again and asked whether the team could return to the sequence they normally used.

“What's wrong with this one?” Thomas asked.

“It's not how we load that route.”

They checked the actual consignments. The established sequence had developed around a customer no longer on that route. With the present load, the revised arrangement gave them better access at the early stops without introducing the original problem. Dennis accepted it.

His first objection had protected the work. His second had needed examination. Both belonged to a competent person.

What an approval contains

We often recognise expertise through visible difficulty. The expert can produce something we cannot: a convincing design, an elegant explanation, a diagnosis of a stubborn problem. When a system produces similar-looking work quickly, the old signal becomes harder to interpret.

A competent approval contains a claim about fitness for a situation. It says that the important conditions have been considered closely enough for the work to proceed. An instrument may check one condition, a colleague another, and a model may help compare the options. Whoever gives approval must decide whether that evidence is sufficient for the proposed action.

A master makes distinctions that alter what happens. This case is routine; that one deserves investigation. This variation is harmless; that apparently small difference changes the whole answer. This procedure remains sound under the new conditions; that rule has outlived its reason.

The distinctions need not arrive as a lecture. Dennis could show the problem by standing beside the goods. A maintenance specialist may hear something unusual before being able to explain its source. A good negotiator may recognise that an agreeable answer contains no actual commitment. The knowledge is useful because of what it allows someone to notice and do.

Make the difference visible enough

When an expert says a proposal is wrong, ask which difference would make it acceptable. This is a more revealing question than asking for an elaborate account of the expert's method.

An expert may be unable to explain a judgment fully. In that case, examine the track record: how similar judgments have fared against alternatives, what they predicted, where they proved reliable and what mistakes cost. A person unable to explain a perception may still be reliable in a narrow setting. Someone able to explain everything smoothly may not be reliable at all.

Generated explanations deserve their own attention. An account of why an answer is right is additional output, and if you treat its plausible sequence of reasons as a record of how the answer was produced, you may give the same untested claim two chances to persuade you. Examine the explanation and the result against the work.

The builder faces his own test

The same question arose in Thomas’s own work. He knew where Northline’s booking software was difficult to maintain because he had written some of it.

He remembered the awkward requests, the changes made after somebody discovered an exception and the small decisions that prevented larger problems. When a system failed, people called him, and he disliked the interruptions in the way a person dislikes something that is also the clearest evidence they have of being needed.

Now he was comparing his proposed booking extension with a service Northline could buy.

The supplier’s product did not fit every case, but it handled several routine tasks well enough to make rebuilding them hard to justify. Thomas could now use an AI coding assistant to write his own version faster. At first, that made him more determined to build it.

Northline needed a dependable booking function. Thomas wanted to remain the person who had built it. Both desires could fit inside an apparently objective comparison, especially when assistance made his own extension quicker to write.

The purchased service was not automatically the better choice. He would have to examine its limits, costs and dependencies. But he noticed how quickly he wanted its shortcomings to be decisive.

Thomas listed what Northline relied on him for. Some items were activities: write an integration, repair a failed transfer, create an internal tool. Others described outcomes: keep booking information dependable, choose systems the company could operate, ensure that a change did not break an existing promise.

If a bought service could handle a routine function, he could spend more time on the decisions specific to Northline. If it introduced a dependency the company could not manage, he could explain that with evidence. His authority would come from understanding the arrangement, including its costs after purchase, rather than from ensuring that his own code occupied every important place.

He still had to do difficult technical work. Selecting, connecting, testing and maintaining systems can demand substantial competence. Describing the shift as simply becoming more strategic would have concealed what he actually needed to learn.

A useful transition names the new work closely enough to attempt it. “Move up the value chain” tells a person almost nothing about Monday morning. “Compare how these two systems preserve booking amendments when a transfer fails” gives Thomas a real piece of responsibility.

When I say leadership begins with truth, I include the awkward truth about what we want a comparison to prove. Thomas owes the business an answer that can survive his preference for building. The loading plan has already required that discipline from Dennis.

Release the method without erasing its history

Northline's internal systems had served a business with different options. Thomas had built things because buying them had been unsuitable, unaffordable or impractical at the time, and a changed choice now did not make that earlier work a mistake, any more than a bridge becomes a mistake when the river moves.

I want experience to matter, particularly after spending years acquiring it. But comfort is a poor way to establish a capability.

If a new system does the work better, I owe it a fair examination. I also owe the experienced person more than a speech about adaptability. Their method may have served the business well and taught people what to notice. Losing its place as the best method does not erase that contribution. I want to hold both thoughts when the experience being examined is my own.

Reliability depends on the work around the model

A builder’s attachment to a system may reflect more than pride in having built it. It can also reflect work that a demonstration rarely shows: records cleaned, inconsistent labels resolved and difficult test cases retained. When you compare systems, ask what would happen to that work if you changed suppliers.

Building machine-learning systems has taught me to ask about the work around the model. Who chooses the information it receives? Who decides what a good result looks like? Who checks the failures that an overall score can hide? If results worsen, who finds out whether the customers’ circumstances have changed or the software has stopped receiving the right information? Those choices help determine whether the system is dependable.

Ask the technical team for a case that could look successful in a demonstration and fail in ordinary use. Did the demonstration give the model information that would not be available when the real decision must be made? Was the model taught to copy previous decisions, even when those decisions may have been wrong? Predicting what someone decided is different from establishing what they should have decided.

Builders can disagree about those choices without either side being afraid of progress. They may be trying to answer different questions about the same system. Make the disagreement concrete enough to fund the work that could resolve it.

I am interested in increasingly capable models. I also want the person buying a result to see how much of its reliability is supplied by people whose work never appears in the product name. Ask for their evidence, and leave them time to produce it.

A task carries several things

At Northline, the proposed purchase would not eliminate Thomas’s job. But building systems had earned him people's trust; buying one changed where he would demonstrate his value. A task can pay a person in more than salary.

Thomas had to compare the options fairly, including his own work. His attachment to it was understandable, and a new title would not by itself make the changed role worthwhile. In other situations, a change may also reduce someone’s income. Training can prepare them for new responsibilities; it cannot by itself replace lost pay.

Thomas's technical objection deserved a technical answer; his preference for building, an honest account of what the business needed. Neither was merely an attitude problem. A person can understand the technology and still object to the terms of change. Answer the objection on its merits. Neither technical confidence nor fear of the future tells you whether the terms are fair. Even a mistaken prediction does not remove their interest in what happens next.

There is no obligation to love every future version of your work. Someone who accepts the business's reasoning might still choose a role elsewhere because its hours or responsibilities fit their life better.

The organisation owes that person a clear account of its needs, the support it can provide and the terms available. It cannot demand that its preferred direction become the organising purpose of another person's life.

Expertise can move

I used to believe that human intelligence would not be replaced. I no longer regard that as a dependable assumption. If intelligence has been our reason for expecting a permanent place above the tools we build, we may be in for a shock. This does not tell me which particular role will change next. It changes the foundation I am willing to offer a reader: human worth cannot depend on winning an indefinite contest of capability.

Suppose a future system identifies the loading constraint before Dennis does, offers the better sequence and explains the changed customer pattern accurately. Would the principle in this chapter fail?

If the system's performance supports reliance in that setting, use it. If its scope expands, reconsider the work. Do not protect a person's status by making everyone ignore a more capable method. Equally, do not infer dependable performance across an entire occupation from a persuasive result on one task.

The point of mastery is the work done well, including the capacity to recognise when conditions have changed. It would be strange to define mastery as a permanent right to be the best available source of every answer.

For the experienced person, this can be a difficult adjustment. Being needed has often provided evidence of being valuable. When someone obtains a useful answer without your help, it can feel like a verdict on years of effort. Yet those years may now support a different contribution: choosing consequential problems, recognising unusual cases, improving a method, or accepting a new system's superiority where it has been established.

These are possible contributions, not promised refuges. They must earn their place too. A book about change should not comfort people by assigning them tasks that machines supposedly can never reach.

When experienced users misread a gain

In METR's early-2025 experiment, 16 experienced open-source developers worked on 246 real tasks in familiar repositories. Tasks were randomly assigned to allow or disallow AI assistance. Allowed assistance increased completion time in that setting, although developers believed it had sped them up. Expertise and a sincere impression of usefulness did not settle the productivity claim.[1]

The study describes those developers, tasks and tools at that time. It does not settle whether coding assistance is useful elsewhere or now. In February 2026, METR explained that differences in who joined its later study and which tasks they attempted made a reliable comparison difficult.[2] As tools change, test them again on relevant work rather than treating either an old disappointment or a new demonstration as the final answer.

A comparison with an answer you may dislike

When Thomas returned to the purchase comparison, he wrote a criterion before finishing it: “If the bought service preserves confirmed bookings and amendments through an interrupted transfer, gives us a usable export, and leaves less maintenance after integration, recommend buying the routine function.” A missing feature would count against it only if Northline needed that feature for an actual commitment.

He put his own extension through the same interrupted-transfer case. This was uncomfortable in a useful way. His design had exceptions too; he had simply been picturing himself nearby to resolve them. The comparison was still open, but he had stated what result would justify choosing something he had not built.

Peter gave him time for it. He did not add it to an unchanged list and call the extra burden an opportunity. Nor did he require Thomas to declare that he had become a different kind of professional before he had done the work.

Return to the loading-plan trial. Asking Dennis to approve every AI-generated plan would add an unlimited checking task to his depot work. Any review arrangement needed to specify which unfamiliar loads required him, give him time to examine them and let him stop a departure when information was missing. Routine loads could use agreed checks.

Meanwhile, on the depot floor, Dennis gathered labels whose important information was difficult to find. He used a general-purpose AI assistant to organise the examples, removed a suggestion that did not fit the floor, and brought the comparison to Thomas. He wanted the labels improved. He did not want to maintain the software.

Earlier, after the revised load had gone out, Dennis had shown a colleague the difference between the first and final arrangement. Thomas had kept the relevant constraint with the planning instructions. They had not turned Dennis's entire working life into a document. They had captured one distinction that had proved useful and one rule that could be retired.

At the end of the week, Thomas still had questions for the supplier. He had also found an interruption his own extension handled only because he had imagined himself nearby to repair it. He left that result in the comparison.

Notes

[1] Joel Becker and colleagues, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, 10 July 2025. Task-level randomisation in an experienced, familiar-repository setting; no inference about all developers.

[2] METR, We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design, 24 February 2026. The later evidence has participant and task-selection limitations.

Section II · Emptying

Choosing what to pursue and what to stop

4. Wanting

Northline is investigating whether AI-assisted booking could make a collection service for small workshops affordable to run. Peter sees many possible improvements. Shaun, who handles customers, begins with a more immediate question: what would a workshop owner actually need the service to do?

One workshop owner did not want a logistics transformation.

She wanted to know whether somebody would collect the goods on Thursday. If they could, she could confirm the job with her customer. If they could not, she needed time to arrange something else.

Shaun, who looked after customers at Northline, had called to discuss a possible new service. He had several questions about booking, tracking and communication. The owner listened until he paused.

“Will I have to call again to find out if you're coming?”

Northline was a regional carrier considering a service for small workshops. Improved software might reduce the administrative work that had made those accounts unattractive. A workshop association was comparing offers and wanted an answer within six weeks. Peter, who ran Northline, could see the commercial opening.

He could also see many others. Thomas, the systems builder, had demonstrated how quickly AI could turn ideas into working screens. Each conversation produced another possibility: a better quotation process, a customer portal, a service for returns, assistance for dispatch. The list was no longer limited by their ability to describe and prototype improvements.

An attractive possibility is not yet a purpose

When developing an idea becomes easier, wanting can feel like working. A leader explores options, obtains a plan and watches a prototype take shape. Yet the colleagues expected to deliver it may still not know which existing work they can stop. Exploration needs room. It also needs a clear decision before an interesting possibility becomes somebody else’s assignment.

Peter initially described the proposed service as making Northline easier for small businesses to use. The statement was agreeable and insufficient. Almost any improvement could fit beneath it. A booking screen, a discount or a broader collection area could all claim to serve the purpose while competing for the same people and money.

Shaun’s conversation supplied a sharper purpose: let a workshop plan around a collection without repeatedly chasing confirmation. The team still had to design a service that could deliver that result at a sustainable cost. But they now knew whose problem they were trying to solve and how the customer could judge success.

What your choice displaces

Shaun brought a second concern to Peter. Existing customers still had unresolved problems. Some had been waiting for an answer while the company discussed how to serve people who were not yet customers.

Northline had already assigned recovered quotation time to following up recurring complaints for a fortnight. That was a real start. Shaun did not want the new opportunity to absorb the same hours before the work was complete.

Peter could have explained that growth would eventually benefit everyone, but a promise about a later benefit would still leave Shaun waiting for the time already committed to his customers; instead Peter had to decide which commitments would receive capacity now.

He protected the customer follow-up allocation. Thomas would first remove a duplicate-entry step that was consuming time in ordinary bookings. Work on an elaborate customer portal would wait. The workshop proposal would first state exactly what Northline could promise to collect and what the team needed to learn before offering the service.

A leader's real priorities become visible in what other people are authorised to stop. When a new purpose arrives without anything leaving, employees must decide privately which customer waits, which colleague receives less help and which unfinished task follows them home, even though the organisation has announced a shared direction. The nearest or loudest demand becomes the working priority.

Who is entitled to make the promise?

At Northline’s next review of the proposed workshop trial, Miriam, a board director, joined the discussion. She was not there to select booking colours or supervise dispatch. The board had an agreed role in commitments that changed the firm's financial exposure.

Peter could approve the initial workshop trial within the budget and existing transport capacity already set aside for it. He could stop the trial without committing Northline to a continuing service. A larger trial, new long-term transport commitments or work outside those limits would need board approval. Miriam would organise that review and make sure the board had the operating and financial information it needed.

Miriam asked what they hoped to know when the pilot ended. Peter began with the potential market.

She put down her pen.

“The pilot, Peter.”

He looked at Thomas, who was trying to straighten a curled corner of the printed proposal. Thomas kept straightening it.

They settled on a more useful answer: whether a defined collection offer could provide enough dependability for customers to pay for it, at a cost Northline could sustain. A favourable response would justify another decision. It would not establish every condition for growth.

A worthy need can still be the wrong work for you

There are people Northline could help in principle but could not serve economically under the proposed arrangement. That fact need not discredit the need or the company. It does require plain language.

It helps to distinguish three commitments. Caring makes a problem worth attention; investigation commits some time and resources to discovering an answer; a promise allows another person to arrange their own work around a result you have undertaken to provide. Moving between them needs evidence and an explicit decision.

This also protects useful ambition. If an investigation is treated as a permanent promise, leaders will avoid examining uncertain needs. If every promise is later described as exploration, customers will pay for the organisation's freedom to change its mind.

Start with the need

Peter's portal proposal had to earn its place against the problems customers already needed solved.

Cheaper problem solving can reveal neglected opportunities. It can also tempt a company to pursue whatever its tool makes easiest. A system that produces presentations quickly can lead to more presentations. A system that builds applications quickly can make every problem look as though it needs another application. Start with the need, not the output you can most easily produce.

Start outside the menu. Who cannot presently do something important? What prevents them? Which of those obstacles has become easier to overcome? Only then ask what the available tools make possible.

On the active list, Peter crossed out the portal. The existing customer problems retained their time. The duplicate-entry improvement came first. Beside the workshop investigation he wrote its owner and deadline.

Then he left the list alone.

5. Taste

Thomas is using AI to produce possible booking screens for Northline’s proposed workshop service. Shaun has to judge whether customers will understand what those screens promise. To see the problem before we return to their test, consider a similar choice in a repair service.

In this hypothetical example, a tenant asks a repair service to fix a leaking tap. One screen ends with a green tick and ‘Tuesday selected’; another shows the conditions near the top and makes the tenant acknowledge that the visit depends on availability. Both record only a request.

Which would you release? Predict what the tenant will tell someone arranging to stay at home. Name the cost you would accept to make that understanding more dependable. You may decide that neither version is ready.

Back at Northline, Shaun faced the same distinction between requesting a collection and confirming one. He preferred the plainer of two designs.

The team was preparing a small-workshop collection service. They had postponed a full customer portal. Thomas, who built the systems, could use AI assistance to make simple booking prototypes quickly enough to examine how an offer might work.

One version looked finished. It had a clear progression, generous spacing and a prominent confirmation button. Shaun disliked the way a selected collection day appeared before capacity had been agreed. A customer might reasonably assume the booking was confirmed.

He proposed a plainer version. It put the conditions near the top and required the customer to acknowledge them.

In Northline’s prototype test, a workshop owner worked through Shaun’s version. At the final screen, she asked whether somebody was coming on Thursday.

Shaun pointed to the distinction between a request and a confirmed collection.

“Yes,” she said. “Which one have I just done?”

His version contained the explanation. It had failed to communicate it at the moment it mattered.

Beyond the ability to spot polish

Taste is often described as knowing what is good. That leaves out the difficult part: good for whom, in what use, against which alternatives, and at what cost?

A finished-looking artefact can make those questions harder to ask. Its completeness suggests that the underlying decisions have already been made. People begin discussing colour, wording and preference while the important uncertainty remains concealed beneath a credible surface.

AI can help a team produce many more designs before committing to an expensive build. But a set of polished options can draw everyone into choosing a design before they have decided whether the proposed service should be built at all. It also makes it possible to spend a week choosing among polished versions of the wrong arrangement.

Shaun had noticed a real problem in the first screen. His mistake was assuming that the opposite appearance would produce the opposite result. Plainness was his preference. Understanding was the required outcome.

This is a common failure of experienced judgment. We learn to distrust a particular kind of bad work and begin using its absence as evidence of quality. A short document must be clear because the last confusing one was long. A restrained design must be trustworthy because the flashy one exaggerated. A handmade process must be careful because an automated one once failed.

Set a standard your preferred design might fail

Shaun's underlying concern was sound. A customer needed to know whether the company had accepted the collection. The interface should make that status unmistakable and show what would happen next.

Once he expressed the standard that way, the team could compare alternatives without defending a style. One version might communicate the status through the main heading. Another might separate the act of requesting from the later confirmation. The question was what a customer would understand and do.

They gave the next workshop owner a situation rather than a demonstration: arrange a collection for Thursday, then explain what you would tell the person waiting for the goods. They watched where she hesitated. They asked what she expected next. They did not begin by explaining the distinction they were trying to test.

A demonstration in which the designer supplies the missing interpretation can make an unclear product look successful. It tells you how the product works with its author standing beside it. That may be a useful service, but it is not the same service as a customer booking alone.

The revised screen began: Request received — collection not yet confirmed. Below it: “We will email you when Northline has accepted the collection. Until then, do not rely on a Thursday pickup.” Asked what she would tell the person waiting for the goods, the workshop owner said she was still waiting for Northline’s answer.

Shaun did not like how blunt the heading looked. The workshop owner understood it.

Return to the repair screen. Either visual style could work, but requiring acknowledgment is not evidence that the tenant understands the final status. Before release, watch someone use it without explanation and ask what they will arrange around Tuesday. Strong evidence concerns the decision they make, not their approval of the design. A slower screen may be a reasonable cost; an extra step that changes nothing is not automatically a virtue.

There is usually more than one kind of good

The customer may prefer instant confirmation. Northline may be unable to provide it until capacity is reserved. A screen that produces the highest immediate satisfaction might therefore create a promise the operation cannot keep.

Judging the screen requires more than asking which version people prefer. Customers must understand whether Northline has accepted their request. Dispatch must be able to rely on the confirmed booking. Staff need a usable record if something goes wrong. Thomas needs to know whether a software change alters what the customer is being promised. A good design must serve those needs together.

Some requirements conflict. Giving every detail can overwhelm the reader. Omitting detail can conceal a condition that would change the decision. Reducing steps can make a task accessible, or remove the moment in which an expensive action is understood. There is no general rule that the shortest journey is the best one.

Someone has to make the trade-off and explain its basis. That is part of the work a leader should expect from people claiming strong judgment. “It feels better” can be an honest starting point. It cannot carry every consequential approval.

Learn from comparisons, including your own mistakes

Keep pairs: the strong version beside the plausible weaker one, the decision that worked beside the one that failed for a reason you now understand, the sentence a customer understood without help beside the sentence you had to explain. Record the difference that mattered.

These comparisons help the team remember what it has learned. Cheap generation makes that habit more important: when producing another version is easy, people may replace a weak design without discovering why it failed. Keep the lesson, not just the latest file.

Shaun's rejected screen belonged in the record. It showed that placing an explanation near the top did not guarantee that the customer would carry it through the interaction. Keeping that lesson was more useful than keeping only the final design and forgetting why it existed.

An AI assistant can help construct alternatives and identify differences. It can also simulate objections. Use that work to widen examination. When the standard concerns what a particular person understands, wants or can operate, that person remains an important source of evidence. A generated account of their reaction is a hypothesis about them.

Do not make your preference everyone's obligation

A leader's taste carries power whether or not the leader intends it to. People can soon learn which format gets praised, which vocabulary sounds serious in the room and which kinds of work get set aside before anyone has tried using them, and find themselves producing for the person at the head of the table rather than for the customer who will never sit at it.

Make room for a version you do not personally like to prove useful. Let someone ask which consequence your objection refers to. If the answer is aesthetic preference, say so. There are decisions in which preference legitimately decides the matter. There are others in which it should receive less weight than accessibility, reliability or the recipient's needs.

This does not require flattening every distinctive choice into a survey result. Good work sometimes asks people to learn a new convention or accept an unfamiliar form. The question is whether the change earns that effort. You can back a strong judgment and still say, out loud and before the result is in, what would show you were wrong.

What becomes scarce when everything looks ready

As plausible output becomes easier to obtain, an organisation may become rich in options and poor in articulated standards. Its debates then grow longer precisely when production becomes faster. People argue over results without agreeing on the work those results must perform.

At the end of Northline’s screen tests, Shaun approved a version he had not initially preferred. He could explain why it was better. More importantly, a workshop owner could explain whether a collection had been confirmed without asking him.

6. Doubt

Before Northline can trial the workshop service, the team needs a route that fits customers’ collection times. Thomas has asked an AI assistant to suggest routes using the addresses and opening hours they have. Ava, who manages the budget, is checking the assumptions before the company commits a vehicle and driver.

Ava did not doubt every number in the route proposal. She doubted the closing time.

Thomas had used the AI assistant to assemble possible routes from customer addresses and estimated collection windows. There were several versions, with enough detail to make choosing among them feel like the remaining task.

The promising afternoon route assumed that the workshops would still be open when the vehicle reached them.

“Where did these hours come from?” Ava asked.

A mixture of public listings and old customer records. Thomas could check the route calculations again. He could obtain a comparison from another system. Neither would establish whether somebody would be at the workshop when the driver arrived.

Ava asked which part of the proposal would change if the hours were wrong. Enough collections would then become impractical that the service would need a different arrangement.

That made the next piece of work clear. They needed to establish the hours with the prospective customers before spending more effort comparing routes.

I began this book to understand a change while it was forming. That puts a limit on the kind of certainty I can offer: a useful principle must help us act before the whole picture is settled, as well as help us stop when an important condition is missing. Scrutiny earns its place by helping us tell the two apart.

Scrutiny has a budget

Doubt is useful when it directs attention towards something that can change a decision. It becomes expensive when it spreads evenly over everything.

A leader facing an unfamiliar capability may alternate between two unhelpful responses: accepting an impressive result because checking it seems difficult, then demanding exhaustive reassurance about the next proposal because the first experience made every remaining uncertainty feel irresponsible. Both avoid deciding what deserves examination.

Start with the consequence of being wrong. A mistaken heading in an internal draft and a mistaken promise to a customer do not deserve the same process. Then ask whether the uncertainty affects the present choice. A forecast may contain many imprecise inputs while depending heavily on only one or two.

At Northline, knowing the exact travel time on every leg would have improved the model. Knowing whether customers were available would determine whether the proposed route was worth modelling in that form. One uncertainty had priority because resolving it could redirect the work.

There are decisions for which a small trial is the best way to learn. There are others for which a trial would expose people to unacceptable harm or create commitments that are difficult to reverse. Doubt should help distinguish them. The phrase “we will learn by doing” cannot decide who is entitled to make other people part of the lesson.

Ask what would reverse the decision

If no plausible fact would change your decision, ask why. The choice may remain sensible across the outcomes you can foresee. An existing obligation may require it. Or you may be refusing to consider evidence against what you want. These are different reasons and deserve different responses.

For Northline’s proposed afternoon route, Ava could state exactly what would change her decision. If enough workshops closed before the planned arrival, the afternoon service would fail the promise Northline wanted to make. A morning arrangement might remain possible. The need for dependable collections would not disappear because the first timing assumption failed.

Shaun contacted the workshops on the proposed route about the specific days and conditions under consideration. He was checking whether customers on that route would be available at the proposed times, not estimating demand across the region.

Agreement can contain the same mistake twice

Thomas had considered asking another model to review the proposal. That could be useful if it exposed a calculation error, a missing alternative or an assumption he had overlooked.

But if both systems received the same closing times, their agreement about feasibility would not independently confirm those times. Two analyses can be different pieces of work resting on the same weak foundation.

Three managers may agree because they have read the same report. If a board then treats their presentations as three independent confirmations, one untested estimate appears to have much more support than it does. Count independent observations, not agreeing voices.

Trace the important claim back to its source. Was the fact observed, reported, inferred or assumed? Does the source have information about this particular situation? Could the agreement have arisen because everyone inherited the same account?

You can put the AI assistant to work on this. Ask it to separate the facts you gave it from the assumptions it needed to reach its recommendation, and then read that second list slowly, because it gives you assumptions to examine rather than leaving them hidden inside a confident answer. It is a starting point. It is not a promise that the system has noticed everything it did not know.

Capability is uneven in ways experience may not predict

In a preregistered experiment with 758 consultants, AI assistance improved performance on a set of consulting tasks but reduced correctness on a different managerial task selected to fall outside the tested system's capability. The work used GPT-4 in a 2023 setting. It supplies a reason to examine the particular task, not a permanent verdict on consulting or later systems.[1]

For a leader, the implication is practical. Familiar difficulty is an imperfect guide to where assistance will be dependable. A system may help with something you consider sophisticated and fail on a nearby task that appears ordinary. Your own success using it in one setting should make you interested in the next setting, not certain about it.

Returning to the workshop proposal, Northline could use AI to develop route alternatives while obtaining availability information from customers. The business did not have to decide whether AI was generally trustworthy before separating these tasks.

Shaun's calls showed that some of the listed hours were unsuitable for the proposed afternoon route. Thomas revised the timing assumptions. The team had not disproved the workshop service. It had prevented one mistaken account of customer availability from organising the rest of the work.

Ava marked the opening-hours question resolved. The workshops ready to commit before the association’s deadline were spread out; Northline had not found enough nearby workshops willing to book together. Sunder therefore proposed fitting their collections into spare time on existing routes. The next test was whether those gaps were enough to provide a dependable service.

The trial would show whether those spare intervals were usable during an actual working week. If the collections needed a dedicated vehicle and driver, the proposed price would not cover the cost.
