Maya needed cases that differed in the fact that changed the decision, not simply more routine requests. Repeating a case Shaun had explained could show that she remembered it. A new case could show whether she recognised the same problem in unfamiliar wording.

Shaun asked her to state the fact that controlled the decision before consulting the suggested reply. She could then ask the AI assistant to examine alternatives and improve the explanation. Afterwards, they compared the response with the decision she had identified.

The sequence mattered. It gave him a view of what she understood, while preserving the tool's useful help. It did not make unaided writing a ritual that every task had to pass. The question was which independent capabilities the role actually required.

If the job requires a person to recognise when to stop, training must establish that recognition. If a reliable tool can perform a calculation the role never needs to reproduce unaided, forcing manual calculation may consume time better spent elsewhere. Independence should follow responsibility, rather than a nostalgia for how the teacher learned.

A lesson costs a piece of today

Northline’s initial plan had been that Maya could ask Shaun whenever she was unsure. After the four-week review and paid handover, his smaller, earlier pattern included scheduled teaching; Nadia covered later cases and served as the alternate supervisor. There was no spare fifth of Shaun’s week waiting to be borrowed.

Peter had two defensible uses for the next available block: shorten the queue of ordinary service requests or let Maya work through exceptions with Shaun. Both helped customers, on different timescales. Shaun could clear the queue faster himself. Maya could not acquire his distinctions by watching it disappear.

Peter protected the teaching block and reduced the routine work scheduled into it. Nadia accepted paid later coverage within her agreed hours; urgent cases went to the designated service cover. Ordinary responses could take longer that day. If the queue began threatening a confirmed promise, they would move the lesson to the next protected slot, record the interruption and reduce intake or buy cover if this recurred. Repeatedly cancelling the lesson would trigger a staffing decision, not become the unrecorded training plan.

That choice does not make learning superior to present service in every case. A commitment that must be kept today can control today’s allocation. The danger is making every day exceptional and discovering, a year later, that the firm still needs somebody experienced.

Let the consequences grow with the evidence

At first, Maya examined cases before a supervisor approved any message to the customer. Later, she handled a defined category herself, with a supervisor available and her decisions reviewed afterwards. Cases outside that category stayed with an experienced colleague. Her authority grew as she demonstrated what she could do.

The progression allowed her to encounter real work without making the customer responsible for discovering the limits of her training. It also prevented her from remaining permanently in simulated exercises where every condition had been selected for convenience.

At Maya’s next supervised review, another customer request put the lesson to the test. This one concerned cartons rather than machinery. They were ready, the customer said, but upstairs; nobody would be available to bring them to the agreed collection point. The AI’s draft reply treated “ready” as sufficient. Maya asked who would move them before the vehicle arrived. She had recognised the same distinction beneath different goods and different wording: readiness for the customer was not yet readiness for the promised service.

The customer arranged to have the cartons brought down. Maya confirmed that arrangement with dispatch and then sent the collection answer. Shaun widened her authority to handle comparable readiness questions under the existing terms. Work involving additional handling still needed a separate decision.

Good apprenticeship gradually makes the learner's reasoning and action dependable under a wider range of conditions. The tools can participate in that development. They should not make the development invisible.

Teaching can follow the question

In a separate learning session at Northline, Maya and Dennis examined recurring instruction problems in customer records. Maya was using AI to group notes with similar meanings. It made patterns visible without reading every entry from the beginning. Dennis recognised that some identical phrases referred to different working conditions.

“You've put all the ready ones together,” Dennis said.

“That was the idea.”

He pointed to an entry. “These goods are packed. But that one still needs permission before it can leave.”

Maya split the group. Then she showed him the wording “awaiting stores approval” in several records he had kept elsewhere. Different phrases recorded the same missing permission to let the goods leave.

“I wouldn't have put those together,” he said.

“The words don't have to match.”

“Neither do the jobs.”

Experience and familiarity with a new method do not always arrive in the same person. An established practitioner may understand the situation deeply while a newcomer knows a more useful way to investigate it. A younger employee may lack the tool knowledge another person assumes they have. An older employee may be the most fluent user in the team.

The task should determine whose knowledge is needed. Age, tenure and novelty are incomplete credentials. Dennis knew why “packed” and “released” described different jobs. Maya knew how to find related cases whose words did not match. They did not need to settle who was generally more knowledgeable before either could teach the other.

A good teaching relationship allows the direction to change with the question. Dennis could lead the explanation of a loading condition and then become the learner when Maya demonstrated a better comparison. Taking that correction did not erase his experience. Accepting his correction did not put her method back under his permanent control.

The experienced person may hear a new method as an attack on their competence. The newcomer may hear an objection as resistance to change. They start defending themselves instead of examining the proposal. The shared question disappears.

Give the exchange time and an object. Maya and Dennis had an allocated period to examine a defined set of records. They were not expected to answer every question from each other's work indefinitely. Thomas was available for technical issues beyond the method Maya could demonstrate.

They tried the approach on a new set of notes. Maya's method revealed a recurring ambiguity Dennis had not previously seen as a pattern. His added distinction prevented several entries being treated as operationally equivalent. The result was useful because both contributions survived the new case.

Maya then changed part of the grouping again. Dennis initially preferred the earlier version, which matched the way he had explained the work. The revised version made the exception easier for a service colleague to recognise. He accepted it after seeing that use.

Reciprocity had required more than allowing Maya to demonstrate a tool before Dennis delivered the wisdom. Her revision had changed the shared method. Peter could judge the exchange by whether it helped them handle new records, rather than by whether both said they had enjoyed learning from each other.

Dennis looked at the new grouping on Maya's screen.

“Does it have to be orange?”

“You asked me to make the exceptions visible.”

“Visible, yes.”

She tried grey.

“Now I can't see them.”

His phone lit up beside the keyboard. The lock screen showed him at a football match wearing an orange shirt, beneath an orange flag, with something orange painted across his face.

Maya looked at the phone. Dennis turned it over.

“That's different.”

She put the exceptions back in orange. He asked her to make the column wider.

Competence forming in a novice and expertise travelling between colleagues are related, but different. Maya still needed evidence before her booking authority grew. In this comparison, her method could correct Dennis immediately. Giving him credit for experience did not entitle him to be right about the grouping.

A mentor can help by locating the edge of their own experience. They may know what usually fails and be unsure whether a changed system removes that reason. Saying so gives the learner permission to investigate without pretending the past contains nothing useful.

The learner can help by identifying what the new method actually establishes. A rapid comparison of records may reveal a pattern worth checking. It does not automatically establish the cause of the pattern or the action the business should take.

A strong mentor should be able to watch a learner adopt a method they do not personally use, or eventually leave for work they would not have chosen. Teaching has enlarged another person's capacity when that person can exercise judgment beyond the teacher's preferences.

At the end of their session, Dennis asked Maya to leave the earlier grouping open beside the new one. He wanted to try the next set of notes himself. Maya moved her chair rather than take the keyboard back.

Note

[1] Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, Generative AI at Work, Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2025. The study's customer-support setting does not establish all forms of durable expertise.

Section V · The Relationships

Collaboration, external promises, and trust

15. Colleagues, and What Is Left When the Transaction Goes

Thomas often went down to Northline’s depot floor to fix a printout, a missing detail or a booking problem. AI-assisted booking and the shared records described earlier have removed some of those interruptions. Over the next few weeks, he discovers that the visits had also helped him understand the depot’s work. Dennis’s proposal to improve the labels brings that loss into view.

For the first week, everyone enjoyed the space. Thomas finished something before lunch. Dennis stopped waiting for corrections to printouts that should have been right the first time.

By the third week, Thomas had stopped knowing which mornings were difficult in the depot. He still had the figures. What he no longer heard was Dennis setting down his mug beside a consignment and saying, “While you're here.” Sometimes what followed had nothing to do with the repair. Sometimes it explained the whole week.

Thomas returned to the label proposal Dennis had begun in Chapter 3. Dennis had used an AI assistant to organise examples of confusing labels into a clear request. Thomas understood the stated change and estimated the work. He could not tell why Dennis had put it ahead of everything else.

He opened a meeting invitation, then closed it. He went downstairs.

The answer emerged when they stood beside a consignment together. Its label said the goods were packed. A smaller note said they were still awaiting permission to leave. Colleagues kept reading the first statement as clearance to load the goods for departure. Dennis had spent part of the morning pointing out the second.

“The printer's working,” Thomas said, half to himself.

“Yes,” Dennis said. “It keeps printing it.”

Thomas laughed, then asked Dennis to show him the next case.

When a teammate's contribution moves

A preregistered field experiment at Procter & Gamble, published in 2026, assigned 791 professionals working on product-innovation challenges to work alone or with another professional, with or without AI. Individuals with AI matched the performance of teams without it on the study's tasks. Assisted proposals also combined commercial and technical perspectives more evenly.[1]

The study challenges the idea that every task requires the same collaboration as before. On those innovation exercises, AI supplied some of the benefit of another specialism. That does not show that it replaces the continuing relationship needed to launch, maintain and answer for real work. At Northline, the question was what Thomas and Dennis learned through working together that the new tools did not provide.

I do not want to defend a meeting simply because people used to need it. I do want to know what becomes harder to see when it goes. Thomas could read every ticket and still miss why the labels mattered so much to Dennis that morning.

To me, this is part of knowing the truth without performative abstraction: sometimes you have to stand beside the person doing the work before the written account makes sense.

Useful dependence can carry something else

It would be foolish to preserve a broken process so colleagues have a reason to talk. The useful question is what knowledge or mutual regard was travelling through the old contact, and whether the organisation now has a better way for it to develop.

At Northline, the requests submitted to Thomas were becoming his main account of the depot. People who could not spare the time to describe a problem disappeared from that account. Their workarounds remained.

Give people something worth doing together

When they discussed the lost contact at Northline, Peter’s first thought was to arrange more informal time together. The team had spent a great deal of time changing work, and a shared lunch seemed easier than another operating decision.

Dennis asked whether lunch meant sandwiches. Peter said he had not got that far.

Thomas had already arranged to look at the labels. They could eat afterwards.

Thomas and Dennis instead took joint responsibility for a small label revision. Dennis would identify the distinctions that mattered in use. Thomas would develop alternatives that fitted the existing system and could be maintained. They would examine the result during an ordinary period on the floor, with time allocated for the work.

During the comparison, Dennis kept straightening the sample labels until their edges lined up. Thomas placed the next one crookedly without noticing. Dennis straightened that too.

Thomas spotted the problem in the first revised label: “Packed” was still the most prominent status, including on goods awaiting permission to leave. Dennis agreed that this made a consignment still on hold look ready to go. In the next version, permission to leave had its own clear place on the label. Packing status remained visible, but no longer stood in for approval.

Credit is part of the relationship

Thomas’s first update called the label revision a systems improvement. That described where the change was implemented, but left out Dennis’s contribution. Credit can disappear this way without an explicit falsehood: the completed work is named after the team that finished it.

Dennis had identified the problem, assembled the cases and helped distinguish a useful solution from a merely different one. If that contribution disappeared every time work entered a technical system, the organisation would learn that only implementation counted as authorship.

Thomas named the joint work in the update. Dennis did not need a ceremony. He needed the record to reflect what had happened.

AI assistance can make this question sharper. A person may turn another's rough observation into a convincing artefact very quickly, and the polished result can make the original observation disappear from view just as easily as crediting only the idea can erase the work of making it usable. Describe the actual contributions specifically. The aim is an accurate account, not a contest to locate one heroic author behind collaborative work.

Colleagues are allowed to have boundaries

An organisation can recognise the value of relationships and then overreach: constant availability becomes evidence of commitment, public enthusiasm becomes evidence of belonging, and personal disclosure becomes evidence of trust, until a person who does their work well but keeps a private life appears deficient. Connection has acquired compulsory terms.

Useful collegiality does not require friendship on demand. A colleague should be able to rely on your part of a shared task, ask a reasonable question and disagree without being treated as disloyal. You do not owe the organisation every part of your private life to make those things possible.

For the label project at Northline, Dennis wanted the problem fixed. He did not want to join every software discussion. Thomas wanted better contact with the floor. He did not want every informal conversation to become an unrecorded development commitment. They agreed where new requests would go and when a situation merited looking together.

Some relationships become less frequent when the old transactions disappear. That can release time for other people or for life outside work. The organisation need not restore every conversation; it needs to notice when losing the conversation also loses a way to understand the work.

When Thomas and Dennis finished the revision, the label was unremarkable to a customer receiving a carton. On the floor, people needed fewer explanations. Thomas and Dennis knew why it looked the way it did, and each knew that the other had helped make the answer worth using.

Note

[1] Fabrizio Dell’Acqua and colleagues, The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI and Teamwork, Organization Science, published online 12 June 2026. This uses the published 791-person account, not the earlier working-paper sample. The result concerns innovation challenges, not demonstrated product-market returns.

16. Clients, Vendors, and Who Did the Work

Thomas’s comparison of building and buying booking software has reached a supplier demonstration. The proposed service uses AI to interpret customers’ requests and handles routine bookings within Northline’s rules. Buying it could reduce the software Thomas has to maintain. Ava, who manages the budget, wants to see whether Northline could recover its records and keep operating if it later left the supplier.

The booking supplier's demonstration ended with a booking confirmed in seconds.

Ava asked to see the booking leave the supplier's AI system.

The salesperson showed her the customer notification.

“I mean the record,” she said. “Suppose we stop using you.”

Northline was considering a bought service for part of its routine booking work. Thomas had compared it with extending the company's own systems. The product offered useful capability, and buying it could release his time for work specific to Northline.

The attractive monthly charge was easy to understand. The future cost of dependence was less visible. Ava wanted to know which records Northline could obtain, in what form, and whether the operating history would still make sense outside the supplier's interface.

The chain behind the promise

A customer buying a collection from Northline does not need to know every tool involved in arranging it. They need to know what the company has promised, which conditions attach to the promise and whom to ring when it fails, and they need those three things in that order and in words a person could read aloud to a colleague while the colleague is holding the phone.

Consider a possible chain: a customer’s AI assistant requests a change, the carrier’s software interprets it, an outside provider processes part of it, and dispatch acts. Each system might report that its step succeeded even though the organisations disagree about what was promised. The customer still needs to know who will resolve that disagreement.

During Northline’s discussions about automated booking, a customer asked Shaun a direct question: if two automated systems confirmed incompatible instructions, who would answer the phone?

Shaun could not promise that the software would sort it out. The customer had bought a collection from Northline. If Northline’s suppliers disagreed about the booking, Northline still had to resolve the problem and answer for its consequences.

The same principle governs Northline as a buyer. A named supplier may rely on other services. Ava needed to know which dependencies could affect the promised function and what support the contract actually provided. A reassuring brand could not answer those operational questions by itself.

What the method changes

Some buyers care principally about the result. Others have legitimate reasons to care how the work is produced: confidentiality, rights, reliability, professional obligations or the circumstances in which a person will examine a decision.

Relevant disclosure should help them decide. If a buyer must approve where confidential material goes, whether a qualified person examines the result or what work an invoice represents, those are the facts to make clear before agreement; listing every incidental tool can bury them.

The useful test is whether knowledge of the method alters the buyer's reliance, rights, cost or available remedy. If a customer's information will be processed in a way their agreement does not cover, the production method is material. If a provider implies that a specialist personally examined work which was never examined, the account is misleading even when the output happens to be adequate.

Northline did not tell customers that every routine message had been personally composed from the beginning. It explained when a booking was confirmed, which changes could proceed automatically and how to obtain help for an exception. Specific information requests or obligations would require more detail. The ordinary service description concentrated on the commitments customers needed to use.

Cheaper production changes the bargain

Suppose a provider can produce a result in a fraction of the previous time. Is the customer entitled to a proportionate reduction in price?

The answer depends on what is being sold and the terms agreed. A price for a completed outcome differs from a charge represented as hours actually worked. A provider should not invent time to preserve an old bill. Nor does every reduction in effort establish that the result has become less valuable to the buyer.

Yet a provider cannot settle the market by declaring that value is independent of effort. If other suppliers offer a comparable result more cheaply, buyers acquire alternatives. If the tool becomes directly usable by the customer, the boundary between buying the service and doing part of it changes.

The provider must explain what remains worth buying: a differentiated result, knowledge of the customer's situation, responsibility for completing the work. Renaming an unchanged output advisory value will not supply any of these.

At Northline, reduced booking effort could improve responsiveness and make smaller transactions worth considering. Customers might eventually demand part of the gain through price. The firm needed to improve its offer and understand its costs, rather than assume the old charge would remain protected by the old amount of work.

Try the exit while the entrance is attractive

Thomas tested exported records for a straightforward booking and for one with changes and an exception. The ordinary record was understandable. In the second, a supplier-specific status label did not explain what had actually been agreed. He needed that meaning documented before Northline could use the record independently.

They asked for an explanation of those fields and tested whether the exported history could support an actual customer inquiry. Ava also examined the agreed notice, support and transition terms. She wanted to distinguish a technical possibility from something Northline could practically exercise under the contract.

Ava also asked who would maintain the connection when either system changed. An inexpensive subscription could still require Thomas's recurring attention. Including that work did not make the supplier's offer unattractive; it made comparison with internal development more honest. Both options needed care after the first successful transaction. The choice depended partly on which care Northline was equipped to provide and which it could sensibly buy.

Thomas recommended buying the supplier’s service for the routine bookings it had been tested to handle. Northline would retain accessible records of its customer commitments and keep responsibility for exceptions. The purchase fitted the approved operating budget. It did not authorise a larger workshop service.

After buying the service, the team rehearsed working without its normal booking screen. Using saved records, they handled the booking and dispatch administration for twelve selected, already confirmed collections over two hours. Other staff continued serving customers outside the exercise. The exercise team could not also manage the normal flow of booking changes. Thomas recorded the tested capacity and the work deferred.

Thomas had recommended buying work he once wanted to build himself. Ava had approved a recurring cost. They could explain why the purchase was worthwhile, and the recovery exercise had shown exactly how much work Northline could support without the normal service.

A remedy should be usable by the person who needs it

A written remedy can be too slow or difficult to help the customer facing the problem. A credit next month may leave today's goods uncollected, and a right to export data may require expertise the buyer cannot obtain during an outage, so that a valuable contractual provision supplies little immediate help at the moment it is most needed.

Examine the experience of exercising the remedy. Who responds, with what information, in what period? What can they actually authorise? Which consequences can be repaired and which must be prevented earlier because repair will be incomplete?

Returning to the recovery exercise, Ava asked Thomas whether the exported records had passed the test.

“The record passed,” he said. “The day wouldn't.”

She wrote the two-hour limit beside the purchase decision. It was an unattractive number to put next to the demonstration. It was the one they might need.

17. Trust

The review of Dennis’s handling target, begun in Chapter 11, is complete. Northline’s AI-assisted report had compared shifts containing different kinds of work as though they were equivalent. While the company investigated, Dennis’s low score remained in use and cost him two weeks of temporary cover for a depot shift lead, work that carried extra pay. Peter now has to explain the correction and what Northline will do about the consequences.

Peter apologised. Dennis waited.

The report compared the number of items employees handled per paid hour. After the customer mix changed, Dennis’s shifts included more mixed loads with heavy items that needed careful placement. The report counted those items in the same way as ordinary cartons. His lower rate therefore appeared to show poorer performance, even though the work itself took longer. Northline’s AI-assisted reporting had made that comparison look settled before anyone checked what happened on the floor.

Dennis had raised the question. Peter had kept the existing assessment in force while the company examined it, believing that a temporary change would treat other employees inconsistently. He had treated the decision about what to do during the review as if it could wait for the review's answer.

During that period, the low result remained in his record. It had excluded him from two weeks of paid relief responsibility for which he otherwise qualified. Other people had seen the flag without seeing his objection.

“I accept that you didn't intend it,” he told Peter. “What happens to the record?”

Reliance needs a basis

Trust is often discussed as a feeling a leader should create. In practical work, it is also a decision to rely on something without personally examining every part of it.

A customer arranges work around a collection promise, a manager assigns resources using a report, and an employee accepts responsibility under an agreed account of how performance will be judged; each relies on work they cannot inspect completely, because no one can verify the whole institution from the beginning each morning.

The handling summary had been used to deny Dennis paid responsibility. Dennis challenged the comparison before the decision, but Northline left the score in force while it investigated. The harm followed because the warning did not change what happened during the review.

Repair the consequence, not only the account

To establish what Northline owed Dennis, Ava and Sunder reconstructed the relevant shifts and decisions. The comparison had not allowed for the changed mix of handling work. Dennis's low flag was removed, and the people who had received the assessment received the corrected account with the reason.

Northline paid the difference associated with the two missed weeks of relief responsibility. It also arranged a suitable paid opportunity to undertake that responsibility, because compensation did not recreate the experience he had missed. The replacement assignment had a real operational purpose; it was not a title invented to complete the apology.

The company checked whether the same comparison had affected other employees. Dennis's willingness to challenge the result should not determine whether everyone else received an accurate record.

Not every harm can be repaired fully. Lost time, a missed opportunity or damaged standing may leave something behind even after a sincere correction. Say what can be restored and what cannot. An organisation should not demand that a person declare the matter emotionally finished because the administrative work is complete.

When Northline made the payment, Dennis checked it against the two missed weeks. It was right. He folded the paper back along its crease.

Peter asked whether there was anything else.

“I told you before the list went up.”

“I know.”

Dennis put the paper away. There was no new information to supply. Peter had received the warning in time to act. The correction did not undo his decision to leave the disputed score in force.

Change the route by which the error acquired power

Northline suspended use of the disputed comparison for consequential assessment while it revised the measure. The operating data could still help identify questions. It would not, in its present form, decide eligibility for additional responsibility.

The revised report separated the kinds of handling work and showed where the information was insufficient for a fair comparison. For a new factual challenge, Ava would arrange a review with Sunder before the next assignment decision. They would tell the employee whether the disputed result could still be used and why. Where the relevant facts could not be settled in time, Sunder would use other documented evidence of the person’s work to decide eligibility. An unresolved score would not, on its own, exclude someone from the paid cover.

This was an internal arrangement, not a claim that every disputed assessment must always be ignored. Some decisions cannot wait, and some objections will prove unfounded. The institution needs to state who decides in the meantime, on what evidence and with what opportunity for later correction.

At Northline, Dennis could identify the shifts and the problem without having to diagnose the reporting system. The company owned the work of investigating its own measure. His role was to supply relevant information and challenge the account, not to become an unpaid auditor before his objection counted.

Trust can become more specific

After a failure, organisations sometimes swing between demanding renewed faith and abandoning a useful capability entirely. A better response distinguishes the different things being relied on.

Dennis could trust the AI assistant he had used to organise his label proposal for that particular task while withholding reliance from the assessment method. The useful tool did not acquit the bad comparison, and the bad comparison did not invalidate every use of assistance at Northline.

Trust can be specific. Confidence should follow the evidence for a particular use and the cost of getting it wrong. Useful work need not wait for anyone to declare an entire person, company or technology trustworthy in every respect.

Inspection has a cost too

Dennis needed Northline to reopen an assessment that had judged his work on the wrong basis. He did not need every collection investigated from the beginning. Neither did the customers whose goods had arrived as promised. Checking everything would consume the time needed to deliver, while asking Dennis to prove the same corrected point again would make the correction worthless. The question is what warrants another look and who can secure it.

The way to reduce scrutiny is to strengthen the basis for reliance and retain a route for correction: keep records proportionate to the consequence, watch for patterns that reveal deterioration, and give a specific exception somewhere to be examined without making every ordinary case pass through a tribunal. Trust needs maintenance too.

What the next disagreement will reveal

At the end of Northline’s repair process, Peter asked Dennis whether the changes addressed the problem. Dennis said they addressed the record and the missed work. He wanted to see whether the challenge route functioned when the next objection came from someone less persistent.

The next objection would test something the exceptional attention to Dennis could not: whether an ordinary employee could get an ordinary error corrected before it cost them work. Peter had a better process on paper. Its next use would supply evidence that he could not obtain by asking Dennis to trust it.

Dennis returned to the relief assignment with the corrected record in place. The payment had reached him. The next person to question a flag would still have to find the reviewer, receive an answer and see what happened to the decision while they waited.

Section VI · The Opportunities

New customers, experiments, and ways to organise

18. The Customers You Could Not Afford

Northline stopped its first collection trial for small workshops because the journeys cost more than the customers would pay. AI-assisted booking made administration cheaper, but it did not shorten the distances between them. A workshop owner has now proposed a different arrangement: a group of nearby businesses willing to share a collection day. Peter and Shaun must decide whether this changes the economics enough to try again.

She brought a map to the meeting with Peter and Shaun.

Northline had already told the association that it would not continue the first collection offer, the trial that failed in Chapter 10. Twelve dispersed workshops had appreciated the service, but the cost of reaching them defeated the price. Some had made arrangements with a rival. Northline had completed its trial and made no promise that a better version would follow.

Now a different possibility had become specific enough to discuss.

Several workshops in a compact area could accept a common collection day if they knew the arrangement would remain dependable. The owner had folded the map so many times that one cluster sat in a tear. She held the edges together and distinguished the businesses she had spoken to from the ones she merely thought might be interested.

“If you can collect on the same day, we can plan around it,” she said. “If the day moves whenever you get a bigger job, we can't.”

Peter could see the route. Shaun, working his agreed earlier pattern, could hear the actual condition of the sale. The customer was offering flexibility in exchange for a promise Northline would have to protect.

The opportunity was not simply that administration had become cheaper. Cheaper administration had made it worth returning to a conversation in which customers could help reshape the service.

Revisit the reason you said no

Every business has customers it once decided it could not serve. An account was too small, a variation too awkward, or an inquiry too expensive to pursue. Over time, those decisions can become rules that nobody thinks to question. Some refusals remain sound. Others deserve another look because the costs have changed.

AI can alter the cost of examining a request, preparing an offer, translating information, coordinating details or supporting a transaction. Those changes can bring previously unattractive customers within reach. The opportunity is to ask which old refusals should now be reopened.

Start with the original reason. If Northline had rejected small workshops because each account required too much individual administration, its improved systems mattered. If the collection still required an expensive journey for a small amount of freight, the software alone would not settle the case.

The first trial had separated those costs. The second proposal changed more than the AI tooling. It combined lower coordination effort with concentrated demand, a common day and a narrower promise. Customers gave up some flexibility. Northline had to provide predictability worth the exchange.

Make the offer small enough to mean

The proposed recurring service included one scheduled collection per workshop per week, up to two ordinary cartons within stated handling limits, carried through Northline's existing regional service. The fee remained $120 per workshop per week. The dollar amounts are illustrative assumptions, not market prices.

Additional cartons, awkward loads and urgent collections required separate terms. They could not quietly consume capacity priced for the ordinary offer. Customers would receive an actual confirmed arrangement, not an optimistic request to be fitted around larger accounts.

The AI-assisted booking process turned differently worded customer messages into a list for the shared collection day. It kept unanswered questions visible, so Shaun did not have to reconstruct each request by phone. Nadia handled later exceptions during her paid coverage. Sunder checked whether the collections fitted the transport plan. The new offer depended on those working arrangements as well as the AI.

The board considered the new trial because it exceeded the first proposal's scope. Miriam brought the operating assumptions, exposure and decision limits into that review. The board authorised a bounded compact-service test with a separate setup allowance of $4,800. That investment was not part of the weekly contribution calculation.

The plan assumed a maximum of 32 workshops within the available capacity band, subject to actual load and time testing. The initial target was 28. A mathematical break-even point would not be treated as sufficient evidence to launch.

Read the economics as a description of the service

The weekly account used the following assumptions for a compact area:

Item Weekly amount ($) at 28 workshops
Revenue: 28 × 120 3,360
Collection transport block 1,850
Handling and onward carriage: 28 × 20 560
Booking and support allocation 190
Expected recovery allowance 180
Defined service cost 2,780
Contribution before wider company costs 580

The collection block is larger than in the first trial, but it serves more customers within a concentrated pattern. The gain comes from the arrangement, not a claim that transport has become free. The support allocation assumes the improved routine process and paid coverage for the work remaining.

Each workshop pays $120 a week and adds $20 in handling and onward-carriage costs. That leaves $100 per workshop to cover the other listed costs, which total $2,220. Within the assumed capacity limit, the weekly amount left before wider company costs is therefore: $100 × number of workshops, minus $2,220.

At 23 customers, the model produces $80 before wider costs. That is a thin mathematical positive. It gives little room for variation and says nothing about recovering the setup investment. Calling it a profitable launch would misdescribe the account.

At 28 customers, the contribution is $580. If Northline charges this service a recurring allocation of $300 for central overhead, $280 remains in this teaching account. The allocation does not imply that those overhead costs disappear if the service stops.

An unexpected additional recovery cost of $400 in a particular week would turn that $280 into a loss of $120 after the allocation. The normal $180 allowance is already in the base model; this example is an extra cost beyond it.

What customers had to agree to

Northline did not enrol 28 names from a map and assume demand had been established. Shaun and Nadia confirmed terms with each prospective customer. Some wanted a different day. Some needed more flexibility than the offer could support. Liking the idea was not enough to count as committed demand. Northline needed to know how many workshops would pay for the collection day it could actually provide.

The workshop owner helped coordinate interest, but she could not commit other businesses without their agreement. Northline obtained each customer's acceptance and kept the ordinary limits clear.

Twenty-eight workshops joined the bounded trial. Their collections ran through the common-day pattern over four weeks. The team recorded actual time, loads, support and incidents, comparing them with the account. Customers paid and had an opportunity to experience the arrangement repeatedly, rather than rate a demonstration.

In the second week, one workshop asked the driver to wait while its final carton was packed. Waiting would have used the interval needed for the next collection. Sunder offered to take the ready carton and leave the unfinished one for the following week's ordinary service, or price a separate collection. The owner chose the first option. He disliked carrying the stock for another week and made sure the next load was ready.

Ava checked whether the service only appeared viable because someone had absorbed extra work without being paid. The incident had consumed support time, which remained in the service record. It had not created an extra journey or unpaid driver work. Across the four paid weeks, transport and support costs fitted the account well enough to continue at 28 customers. The trial had also shown where the margin could disappear: a helpful exception that required an extra journey. The upper limit of 32 remained unvalidated.

Do not spend the same spare capacity twice

The new service relied on existing onward capacity. That capacity had a limit. It could not also be promised without cost to another expansion plan.

An extra customer is attractive only if the additional revenue exceeds the additional demands it creates under the actual conditions. One nearby workshop might fit the present block while another needs a larger vehicle, an incompatible window or a second collection, making two apparently identical increments of revenue buy very different increments of work. The neat linear account would cease to describe the service.

Northline continued with 28 workshops. Any increase in customers, volume, geography or terms needed another review. The board’s permission to test the compact design did not authorise Peter to extrapolate the weekly margin across the region.

The setup investment also remained to be recovered. A positive weekly account did not erase the $4,800 committed to preparation. Ava kept it separate so the company could distinguish a useful ongoing service from the full return on the attempt.

Make a useful service reachable

The workshop owner could arrive with a map, negotiate a common day and pay for a service. Northline's successful offer tells us something about customers who were too expensive to serve. It tells us less about a person who was never considered an account at all.

Think of a clinic that cannot obtain specialist attention for every difficult question, a claimant who cannot afford help assembling an appeal, or a small producer who has to conduct business in a language in which explaining an unfamiliar problem is exhausting. These are directions to investigate, not claims that a current system can safely meet every need. They enlarge the meaning of the question: who can now be helped?

AI may help someone organise their records, identify a missing document or prepare a question in another language. They can then arrive at a service with something a qualified person can use, rather than having to explain the whole problem under pressure. That change is worth building well.

I find this possibility compelling because the gain need not be a cheaper version of a service already enjoyed. It can be a first usable entry into one. A person who arrives knowing which document is missing or which question remains unanswered is in a different position from someone sent away to make sense of the instructions alone.

The workshop lesson still matters. Where preparing the explanation is much of the service, cheaper preparation may remove a large barrier. Where the explanation must lead to a clinical examination, a funded remedy or a qualified decision, that next step needs its own capacity and authority. More prepared requests can make the remaining shortage visible; they do not fill it by themselves.

There is a design choice here. You could use the saved preparation time to process more familiar accounts. You could also reserve some of it for people whose needs used to fall below the threshold for attention, and judge the attempt by whether they obtain a useful result. The price, access route and support would have to fit their circumstances. A service available only to someone with a card, a quiet room and confidence in the instructions has already chosen part of its audience.

Who in your field was never an account? Name a need you could now examine with them, and the person or institution that would have to join you to make the answer useful.

Back at Northline, the workshop owner could confirm her Thursday collection without wondering whether she would spend the afternoon chasing a van. Northline had found a new source of revenue by making that ordinary certainty affordable.

19. The Ideas You Could Not Afford to Test

Northline’s compact workshop service is continuing with twenty-eight customers on a common collection day. Thomas is using an AI route-planning tool to explore other arrangements within that service. Peter asks for more route options. Maya, the service trainee, has noticed a different need in the customer notes: parts and equipment waiting to be returned. This chapter follows the team as it turns her observation into a proposal and a limited test.

Peter asked for more routes from the AI route generator.

Maya asked whether routes were the only thing they should vary.

The first AI-generated options closely resembled the successful route: different collection sequences, slightly different time windows, several ways to use the same block of transport. Thomas could prepare more alternatives than before, but they all began with the same kind of service.

Maya had been examining customer notes. Workshops wanted to send parts and equipment back to their suppliers, but some items could not leave until a repair job was finished. Northline was improving collections of goods already ready to ship. These customers needed a separate arrangement for returns whose readiness depended on the work in progress.

Thomas added return arrangements to the exploration. The possibilities changed more than they had when he asked for another hundred routes.

Search has a shape before it has a size

Making alternatives cheap can improve a decision, but the benefit depends on what is allowed to vary. A large number of answers can occupy a narrow space if they all inherit the same definition of the problem.

Northline initially held the offer, direction and customer behaviour constant. It searched for a more efficient sequence within them. That was useful work. It would not discover a return service unless someone changed the field of consideration.

A leader should examine two costs: the effort required to develop another alternative within the present question, and the attention required to notice a customer need, an unexamined assumption or a different kind of offer that would change the question itself. Cheap variants do not guarantee a wide search.

AI assistance can help with both. It can generate variants and suggest dimensions the team has overlooked. Local observation can supply a need the prompt did not contain. The strongest exploration combines these contributions instead of assuming either the tool or the experienced person must originate every useful possibility.

The potential offer was specific: collect suitable returned parts or equipment under a separate arrangement that reduced repeated coordination for workshops. It required its own handling terms and economics. The existing service made the question worth examining, not already answered.

Spend the gain on wider attempts

When development is expensive, a team may pursue the first plausible idea because comparing alternatives would consume the opportunity. Cheaper analysis and prototyping can make that habit less necessary.

What excites me most is the work that has no before-and-after chart. Imagine a useful idea that has never become a proposal because its owner cannot write software, afford a specialist or justify taking colleagues away from the work already paying their salaries. It survives as an occasional irritation: surely somebody could make this easier.

I am interested in what happens when that person can finally try. The first attempt might disappoint or reveal that the difficult part was elsewhere. It might also produce something ordinary and useful that would otherwise have remained an irritation for years. Our measurements should leave room for things that previously did not get attempted.

At Northline, investigating recurring return problems did not require a research department. It did require someone’s time and permission to explore an idea that might fail. Peter set aside that time and limited the number of active tests. The team could examine many possibilities, but only a few would be allowed to make customer promises or use physical capacity.

Improve the way you tell attempts apart

Andrej Karpathy's 2025 essay on verifiability argues that repeated attempts and usable feedback help explain which tasks can be optimised through neural-network training.[1] His claim concerns a technical mechanism. It also prompts a practical question for a business: how will you tell whether the next attempt is better?

The leadership application is an inference, not something established by the essay. An organisation needs a way to select among proposals that fits the outcome it values. If the test rewards the wrong thing, cheaper search can produce more accomplished versions of the mistake.

Northline showed its first return-service proposal to a workshop owner. It required goods to be ready for collection at closely fixed times. She looked at the proposed window.

“If the repair's finished, you can have it. If it isn't, changing the collection time won't finish it.”

The plan treated release as a choice the customer could make for the convenience of the route. It depended on the completion of another job. More optimisation inside the same assumption would not earn her order.

They changed the offer instead. A workshop would keep the items until the job was finished, then confirm that they were ready to return. Northline would offer a collection time only after checking readiness, the supplier’s acceptance and transport capacity. An unfinished job would no longer be treated as freight that could be moved merely by choosing a better route. Northline was proposing a collection service, not taking over storage or promising that the repair would finish on time.

The preferred proposal became less impressive on the original route measure and more promising as a service. The difference justified another test.

They kept some customer situations outside the initial design work and used them to examine the surviving proposal. A plan repeatedly adjusted to the same examples can become excellent at those examples while remaining fragile elsewhere. The additional cases gave Northline a way to ask whether it had found a useful arrangement or merely accommodated the people already in the conversation. Search needed fresh contact as well as more computation.

I used to think of these systems as stochastic parrots: mimicking their training, however impressively. That description no longer captures what interests me. People often create something useful by carrying lessons from a few domains into another; the possibility that AI can combine knowledge, propose a test, examine feedback and try again has changed the question I ask of it. I now think of a possible tireless investigator, not merely a machine producing the next impressive answer.

The analogy has a condition. Iteration needs evidence capable of rejecting an attractive mistake. A system can keep revising a wrong account as tirelessly as a useful one. My changed view opens more work to investigation; it does not make achieving an arbitrary goal inevitable. Here, the customer's refusal is part of the experiment, and the AI system must have a way to hear it.

The generated change has to survive a contrary case

The return proposal needed a small change to Northline's booking screen: a field recording whether the receiving supplier had accepted the return. Thomas used an AI coding assistant to draft the code and suggest test cases. Previously he would have written the change himself or postponed it behind larger requests. The saving was in preparing something worth examining; the draft had no authority to alter a live booking.

Thomas tested the change on a separate copy of the booking screen. An accepted return appeared as ready. He then recorded that the supplier had withdrawn its acceptance, but the screen still showed “ready.” The code had remembered the earlier yes and failed to act on the later no.

The distinctions were compact enough to show on one page:

Part of the work What it did What it could not establish
Model assistance Drafted code and proposed examples That the examples covered the promise
Ordinary software Stored the latest agreed state, checked permitted changes and ran repeatable tests Which changes Northline ought to permit
Thomas and the operating team Defined the meaning of acceptance, examined failures and approved a limited release That future circumstances would match the test

Thomas corrected the code and kept three cases for future testing: a supplier’s refusal, a withdrawn request and an ordinary acceptance. Each test checked whether the screen showed the correct booking status. The code did not have to look like something Thomas would have written himself; it had to produce the right result. Sunder checked what dispatch would see. Only then did Thomas release the limited change through Northline’s normal approval process. The previous version remained available if the change had to be withdrawn.

A conventional form with a required field could have supplied the same operational rule. AI made preparing and revising the proposed implementation cheaper; it did not invent the requirement or replace the database. The firm's gain depended on having enough attention left to discover that the first implementation was wrong.

If Thomas later used another AI coding assistant to revise the program, he would test the revised code again. Changing the assistant alone would not change software already running at Northline. The assistant helped write the program; it did not have to stay connected for that program to work.

Make important questions cheaper to investigate

The customer's unfinished repair changed Northline's search. It showed why another hundred route variants could be less useful than one better question. A commercial trial makes that turn easy to watch; it cannot convey the value of finding a question whose answer might relieve suffering.

I want to take the possibility seriously without mistaking a promising candidate for a discovery. If a research team can examine a wider field of molecules or materials, obtain useful predictions and select better experiments, the value may lie in attempts it would otherwise never have afforded. The point is not to keep the laboratory busy. It is to make an important uncertainty cheaper to resolve.

Scientists face the same gap between a useful computational answer and a result established in the world. In 2021, the AlphaFold researchers reported strong results at predicting protein structures in an independent assessment called CASP14.[2] This was a substantial advance in a defined scientific task. A prediction could help researchers choose what to investigate without settling every question about what a protein does.

In a companion paper, researchers used predicted human-protein structures to develop biological hypotheses that still needed experimental confirmation.[3] They could investigate more possibilities without treating every suggested mechanism as an established finding.

These systems are specialised scientific AI. Their results are not evidence that an ordinary conversational model can reproduce the same work. For a scientist deciding what to test next, a useful prediction can make a previously unaffordable question worth pursuing.

That is a larger opportunity than producing familiar outputs faster. An organisation that wants this benefit has to get better at turning possibilities into evidence. Otherwise the wider field is just a longer queue of ideas nobody will test.

Materials research supplies another concrete instance. The 2023 GNoME paper combined learned predictions with further computational evaluation to search for stable crystal structures.[4] Its candidate structures do not by themselves establish a manufacturable battery, a useful device or an affordable product. They illustrate how a larger computational search can change the starting point for subsequent work.

For a team choosing an experiment, a better starting point could mean fewer months spent on an unpromising candidate, a neglected hypothesis becoming cheap enough to examine, or a specialist spending scarce laboratory time on the question most likely to distinguish two explanations that had previously looked equally plausible. None is a guarantee of success. Each changes which failure is worth paying to learn from.

That is the fascination I want to carry into ordinary organisations too. Someone may finally be able to investigate the recurring difficulty everyone had accepted because no one could afford to look closely. Ask which important question in your field has been waiting for the cost of asking it to fall, and what evidence would let you spend more on the answer.

Keep the cost of rejection low

Back at Northline, the revised plan was ready for a limited test, not a full launch. The team examined the relevant goods and customer arrangements, defined the types of returns the trial would accept and estimated its cost. Other work remained excluded.

Several proposals stopped before any collection. A customer could not accept the terms. A handling condition added more cost than the expected price would cover. Another variation duplicated a service already available on adequate terms.

Those rejections were useful. The company had obtained information without building a large commitment around each idea. The surviving version received a small authorised test; no general commercial success was declared.

A disciplined search process should let an employee bring forward an unfamiliar idea, obtain a serious test and withdraw it when the evidence fails, without turning that sequence into a verdict on their ability to recognise an opportunity. Otherwise recommendations become more polished as uncertainty becomes less visible.

At the same time, someone has to protect unfamiliar ideas long enough to be examined. Immediate rejection because a proposal does not fit the present categories will keep the search inside the old business. Give the possibility a cheap route to relevant evidence, then let that evidence matter.

Peter's route request had become a small test of a different service. The compact collections stayed within their established scope. Maya had found the question, Thomas had made alternatives cheap enough to compare, and a customer had spoiled the most elegant plan.

The next proposal took account of when the workshop could actually release the goods. Whether enough customers would pay for that arrangement still needed testing.

Notes

[1] Andrej Karpathy, “Verifiability,” 17 November 2025. Researcher interpretation, not an empirical law of business success.

[2] Jumper et al., “Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold,” Nature, 2021.

[3] Tunyasuvunakool et al., “Highly accurate protein structure prediction for the human proteome,” Nature, 2021.

[4] Amil Merchant and colleagues, Scaling deep learning for materials discovery, Nature, 2023. Computational exploration and stability prediction; candidate structures are not equivalent to experimentally validated, manufacturable products.

20. The Organisation You Could Not Afford to Build

Elise runs an independent carrier in the area next to Northline’s. Each company sometimes receives requests the other could serve. Previous discussions about cooperation stalled because clarifying those requests and obtaining answers took too much work. AI can now help prepare the information for a handover. Peter and Elise are considering a limited partnership, but they still have to agree who can promise what.

Elise did not want Northline to buy her business.

She ran an independent carrier in an adjoining area. Her vehicles and people knew that territory. Some of her customers needed collections or deliveries beyond it, just as Northline's customers sometimes needed work beyond Northline's comfortable reach.

Peter could imagine a larger company serving both. Elise could imagine keeping her company and exchanging suitable work through a dependable arrangement.

They had discussed cooperation before. The difficulty was rarely drawing two regions on a map. It was agreeing what each request meant, obtaining a timely answer, preserving the customer promise and dealing with the work that did not fit the ordinary case.

For a typical consignment in the proposed service, Northline would collect the goods in its region and pass them to Elise’s carrier for the next part of the journey. Northline would remain the customer’s contact. Both carriers needed to agree on the goods, the physical handover and their responsibilities before Northline confirmed the service.

Thomas could now show them a clearer way to exchange those booking details. AI assistance helped interpret incoming requests and prepare the information. The shared booking record showed what each carrier had accepted; it did not move the goods or grant permission on the other carrier’s behalf.

The reduced coordination effort made a different organisational possibility worth examining. Northline might reach more customers without owning all the people and vehicles involved.

It would also become responsible for a relationship it could not manage by issuing instructions down its own reporting line.

A firm has boundaries for reasons

Some work is easier to organise inside one company, where people share priorities, authority and resources. Other work is better bought from an independent specialist. Employing people gives you more control, but also the obligation to pay them when demand is low. Buying a service gives you access to someone else’s capacity, but requires agreement each time the work or terms change. If AI makes that coordination cheaper, an arrangement that was once impractical may become worth trying.

A small firm might obtain capabilities that previously required a larger internal team. Several specialists might work together around a shared service. A large firm might integrate more activity because it can coordinate a greater span. The technology does not contain a universal preference for small organisations or large ones.

For the partnership decision at Northline, Peter had three real choices. Northline could continue its local focus and decline work outside the offer. It could invest in owned capacity and management for a wider operation. Or it could develop a partnership in which another firm supplied part of the service.

Each choice created a different business. The comparison had to go beyond which one required the smallest initial team.

Compare the work each boundary creates

Owned expansion would give Peter more direct authority over the operating design. It would also require capital, recruitment, local knowledge and enough demand to support the commitment. The company would acquire the obligation to keep those resources useful when volume changed.

Partnership could provide reach sooner and with less owned capacity. Northline would need to agree terms, exchange reliable information and manage a dependency. It would not control every decision within Elise's firm, and her existing customers would have legitimate claims on her capacity.

Local focus would preserve attention and reduce the risk of diluting an offer that had begun to work. It would also leave some customer demand to others and might limit relationships worth developing.

Ava asked for an account of the full work each option would create. Who would handle the customer inquiry? Who would reconcile inconsistent instructions? What capacity had to be reserved? How would payment and working capital move? Who would absorb a failed handover, and how would that affect the price?

If Elise’s team did coordination work, held capacity or handled exceptions without being paid for them, the partnership would look cheaper than it was. Those costs would still support Northline’s customer promise. They would simply fall on Elise’s business.

Build the relationship around a narrow transaction

Peter and Elise began with one defined class of ordinary consignments between their areas. The first arrangement excluded unfamiliar handling requirements and urgent exceptions. Either carrier could refuse a request before accepting it. Once accepted, the request became a commitment, with an agreed process for resolving problems. Both firms needed to know exactly when that commitment had been made.

Thomas built the handover view from the information both firms had agreed to share for this work, and it recorded four things in a form either side could check: who had asked, who had accepted, on what terms, and what had changed since. AI could reduce the work of interpreting requests and preparing that information. It could not turn a proposed handover into permission to use Elise's capacity.

Peter wanted an ordinary request left unanswered at the cutoff to count as accepted. Otherwise, he said, Northline might lose the customer while waiting.

“You can lose the inquiry,” Elise said, “or I can discover you've sold my afternoon.”

Elise offered a paid period during which her staff would review Northline’s requests and answer them. Payment would cover that review work, even when she refused a request. It would not buy automatic acceptance. Peter agreed: if no answer arrived before Northline needed to reply to its customer, the request would remain unaccepted.

Previously, calls to clarify a small consignment could consume its potential margin before a vehicle moved. In the trial, the shared record supplied the facts and Elise’s paid response period supplied an answer. The firms would proceed only if the customer price covered the transport and coordination costs and left an acceptable return for both. Requests needing repeated individual negotiation fell outside the ordinary offer.

Miriam brought the proposal to the board because it changed Northline's dependencies and the scope of its service. The board authorised a limited test within the defined category, with a budget and exposure limit. It did not approve a general network or unlimited cross-partner exceptions.

The first handovers proceeded under those terms. Customers obtained a service Northline alone would not have offered in the same form. Elise received paid work she could fit into her operation. The two firms learned what information the next handover required without committing to ownership of each other.

Peter could not resolve a later capacity conflict by naming Northline's customer as the most important. Priority would need another negotiation; Elise might refuse even if he offered to pay. The shared screen could show the conflict. It could not settle it.

When Elise could not accept a request, Northline still owed its customer an answer. Her refusal would define what the partnership could offer; it would not become a problem the customer had to resolve between the two firms.

I am excited by the prospect of a small business doing work that once demanded a much larger organisation. But I would not call it progress merely because the staff and vehicles disappear from its own accounts. I want to know who now carries the obligation, whether they can refuse it and whether the price pays for their part. Elise's independence is part of what makes this opportunity valuable. A design that quietly spends it has changed the bargain.

Scale is a choice about repeated obligations

The tempting description of the new arrangement was that Northline could scale without assets. The more accurate description was that it could offer some additional work through paid access to another organisation's assets and competence.

Somebody still had to own the vehicles, maintain them and provide drivers. Those costs remained with Elise’s business. Northline needed an agreement that gave it dependable access to capacity it did not own or control. The partnership changed how the two companies shared costs and risks; it did not make those costs disappear.

The arrangement could nevertheless be an important opportunity. A useful small firm can become more capable without reproducing every function internally. Specialised businesses can reach customers they could not justify serving alone. Shared infrastructure can support diversity of ownership rather than requiring one company to absorb every participant.

Organise around the work you want to make possible

Cheaper coordination can make cooperation practical without requiring two businesses to become one. It also opens a wider question: which useful activity has been waiting for an organisation too expensive to create?

Imagine independent translators, subject specialists and a small publisher considering material none could produce alone. If preparing the source, finding the relevant expertise and reconciling revisions become cheaper, they might be able to pay for an arrangement that a permanent editorial department could not justify. The work still needs permission to use the material, readers who want it and someone answerable for what is published. Those requirements help define the organisation that is actually needed.

Or consider a network of small producers trying to prepare a common response to a buyer. Assistance could help them compare specifications and assemble a proposal while they retain separate businesses. Whether that route works depends on who can commit supply, how disagreement is settled and whether the common promise survives one participant's failure.

I am interested in the space between doing everything alone and employing everybody involved: a project can gain access to expertise, a specialist can reach a worthwhile customer, and several small organisations can attempt something larger without each surrendering the part of the work they know how to govern. That is a possibility to test, not a preferred size of firm.

Some arrangements will need a permanent organisation after all. Repeated disputes, continuing obligations or the need to invest together can make shared authority worth its cost. Discovering that is useful too; it tells you what ownership would be buying.

Put the activity you want to make possible before the organisation chart. Then compare the cost of obtaining agreement, keeping the promise and repairing failure under each arrangement. You may need fewer walls. You still need to know who answers the door.

Back at Northline’s partnership review, Peter slid the map towards Elise. He had drawn the two territories in the same colour.

She turned it over and wrote the response hours on the back. That was the part she wanted to take away.

Northline kept its compact service within the established local scope. It had bought no company and opened no depot. The new reach depended on an agreement worth maintaining on both sides.

Section VII · Diffusion

How change spreads and who receives its gains

21. First a Tool, Then a Different Business

Northline has improved its own booking work with AI, but exchanging information with other businesses still takes effort. Now several customers have begun sending requests in a common format that both Northline and Elise’s carrier can use. This chapter follows that change: how an improvement outside the company makes its existing tools more useful, and what Peter should prepare for next.

The change that made the handover easier did not happen at Northline.

Several customers began sending booking details in the same structure, with the fields both carriers needed. Fewer instructions were scattered across separate messages. Northline’s team could use the information without repeatedly asking customers to reconstruct the request.

Thomas and his colleagues had used AI assistance long before this happened. They already had useful internal tools and helped run a continuing compact-workshop service, relaunched in Chapter 18, and a limited arrangement with Elise's carrier in an adjoining area.

The new customer format did not make the models more intelligent. It made a previously awkward exchange easier to complete. A workflow that had required repeated intervention now worked more smoothly across organisations.

Peter had expected progress to arrive as a better product he could buy. Some of it arrived because other people changed their own work.

Four different events

A person obtains access to a capability. They use it for a task. The organisation changes a workflow around it. The changed workflow produces an economic or service result.

These events are connected, but they are not interchangeable. A company can distribute access, discover frequent individual use and redesign a process around it, yet still fail to earn an adequate return because the changed work costs more elsewhere or creates an outcome customers do not sufficiently value. Each stage has something different to establish.

In a 2025 essay, Andrej Karpathy observed that broad individual access to language-model assistance could coexist with slower organisational change. He pointed to the coordination and integration demands faced by institutions.[1] The useful observation does not require accepting a universal account of technology history or assuming that every individual benefits equally.

Survey evidence offers a related distinction. A study of US adults in 2024 separated trying generative AI, using it at work and using it intensively. Broad reported use did not mean that most working hours were already assisted.[2] Those are dated observations, not a current census of the world.

For a leader, the practical question is where the proposal actually sits. Has somebody demonstrated a capability, or has the business changed the work through which its value would appear?

The missing piece may be elsewhere

Organisations can spend heavily improving their own part of a transaction while the customer still cannot supply the required information, the supplier cannot accept the new format or the physical operation cannot absorb the additional flow. Professional obligations may require a different review as well. Improving the internal task has not removed the external wait.

Progress then appears slow even when the internal technology improves. Several missing pieces may later become available close together, making the transition look sudden.

At Northline, compatible customer instructions complemented work already done on records, authority and partner handovers. Thomas could reuse those arrangements. He did not need to rebuild the whole chain each time another customer used the format.

This gave the change momentum. A customer could see a simpler exchange because the carrier was ready for it. The carrier could justify improving the exchange because more customers could use it. The benefit of one participant's change depended partly on the others.

That interaction can produce rapid movement. It can also fail to begin if each party waits for another to bear the initial cost. You need to identify who benefits, who must change first and what would make that first commitment worth making.

Northline offered a small group of existing customers help with the new booking arrangement. The work was limited and funded. The company could justify it through reduced repeated coordination and a better customer experience, without waiting for every business in the region to adopt the same process.

A lag is not a promise

A disappointing early result can mean the organisation has not yet made the complementary investments required. It can also mean the idea is unsuitable or the expected benefit too small.

Research on the “productivity J-curve” examines why spending on training, new processes and other preparation can come before measurable returns from a technology.[3] It gives a leader a reason to examine that surrounding work. It does not guarantee that a disappointing investment will eventually succeed.

Northline's first dispersed workshop trial deserved to stop. Its failure was not evidence that the firm should fund the same design indefinitely while waiting for a promised technological payoff. The later compact service worked because the conditions changed in specific ways.

Name the missing condition. Who could supply it? What would it cost? What evidence would show it was in place? If the answer is only that the world will eventually catch up, the proposal is still relying on a hope the business cannot schedule or control.

Peter could describe the customer information change and the work it removed. He could also see remaining limits. A compatible booking format did not make Elise's capacity unlimited or resolve every exception between firms. Those conditions needed their own arrangements.

Forecast the next commitment

A useful adoption forecast helps a leader decide what to prepare, when to commit and what to watch. It need not predict the exact year in which an industry becomes transformed.

Begin with the task and the surrounding work. Identify the capability already available, the conditions that prevent routine use and the people who would need to change. Then describe a plausible next stage and the evidence that would justify it.

At Northline, the next stage was broader use of the compatible handover within the existing permitted categories. Evidence would include fewer missing fields, timely partner acceptance and costs that remained consistent with the offer. More messages passing through the system would be insufficient if unresolved exceptions grew faster.

Where useful AI assistance is widely available, I expect more competition to turn on whether businesses can complete work together.
